docs.title: CLI Recipes
docs.text:
Common pymobiledevice3 commands grouped by task. Every command has --help, which lists its arguments and options.

Words in capitals (DIRECTORY, PID, BUNDLE_ID, ...) are placeholders for your own values. A bundle ID is an app's identifier, such as com.apple.mobilesafari; pymobiledevice3 apps list prints them. Commands under developer need Developer Mode turned on, and some also need the DeveloperDiskImage mounted (see Developer Mode and DDI). On iOS 17+ many commands also need an RSD tunnel (the transport iOS 17+ uses for developer services); the CLI sets one up by itself, with no flag and no sudo (iOS 17+ tunnels explains the options).

docs.title: Device Discovery and Connectivity
docs.text:
# List connected devices
pymobiledevice3 usbmux list

# Find iOS 17+ devices advertising RemoteXPC (Apple's developer-service protocol) on the local network.
# On macOS this needs sudo: it pauses the host's remoted while it connects to each device
sudo pymobiledevice3 bonjour rsd

# Forward a host TCP port to a port on the device, over USB
pymobiledevice3 usbmux forward HOST_PORT DEVICE_PORT

docs.title: Logging and Diagnostics
docs.text:
# View all syslog lines (including debug)
pymobiledevice3 syslog live

# Filter syslog lines
pymobiledevice3 syslog live -m SpringBoard

# Exclude syslog lines
pymobiledevice3 syslog live -v unwanted_log

# Capture Bluetooth HCI traffic in PacketLogger format
pymobiledevice3 btlogger trace.pklg

# Capture Bluetooth HCI traffic as pcapng for Wireshark
pymobiledevice3 btlogger -f pcapng trace.pcapng

# Restart device
pymobiledevice3 diagnostics restart

# Pull crash reports
pymobiledevice3 crash pull /path/to/crashes

# Remove only matching crash reports, without copying them
pymobiledevice3 crash clear --match '^MobileSafari'

# Show the process list (no Developer Mode, DDI or tunnel needed)
pymobiledevice3 processes ps

# Match process pids by name (like pgrep)
pymobiledevice3 processes pgrep SpringBoard

docs.title: Network Sniffing (PCAP)
docs.text:
Every packet is labelled with the process that sent it; see Capturing network traffic for filtering by process in Wireshark and tshark.

# Sniff all device traffic and save it for Wireshark
pymobiledevice3 pcap --out capture.pcapng

# Sniff only a given process, stopping after 100 packets
pymobiledevice3 pcap --process backboardd -c 100

# Sniff a single interface
pymobiledevice3 pcap -i en0

docs.title: Files, Apps, and Backup
docs.text:
# Open AFC shell (media directory). Inside it, device commands pipe into host tools and
# redirect into local files: `cat notes.txt | grep todo`, `cat photo.heic > photo.heic`
pymobiledevice3 afc shell

# Offer more host tools inside the shell (any tool also works as `!tool` without the option)
pymobiledevice3 afc shell --tool jq --tool plutil

# List installed apps
pymobiledevice3 apps list

# Query specific app bundle IDs
pymobiledevice3 apps query BUNDLE_ID1 BUNDLE_ID2

# Dump contacts / calendars / Safari bookmarks / mail accounts without a backup
pymobiledevice3 mobilesync dump contacts

# Add or modify records (keyed by record id from `dump`; unknown ids add new records), then delete one
# Use a plist instead of JSON for records with dates, such as calendar events
pymobiledevice3 mobilesync push contacts changes.json
pymobiledevice3 mobilesync delete contacts RECORD_ID

# Full backup
pymobiledevice3 backup2 backup --full DIRECTORY

# Turn iCloud Backup on / off (needs a signed-in iCloud account)
pymobiledevice3 backup2 cloud on

# Preserve only selected backup payloads
pymobiledevice3 backup2 backup --only messages DIRECTORY
pymobiledevice3 backup2 backup --only messages --patch-manifest DIRECTORY
pymobiledevice3 backup2 backup --only sms DIRECTORY
pymobiledevice3 backup2 backup --only whatsapp DIRECTORY
pymobiledevice3 backup2 backup --only contacts DIRECTORY
pymobiledevice3 backup2 backup --only call_history DIRECTORY
pymobiledevice3 backup2 backup --only bookmarks DIRECTORY
pymobiledevice3 backup2 backup --only-regex '\.(plist|db|db-shm|db-wal|sqlite|sqlite-shm|sqlite-wal|sqlitedb|sqlitedb-shm|sqlitedb-wal|storedata|storedata-shm|storedata-wal)$' DIRECTORY

# `messages` keeps sms.db plus the complete SMS/iMessage attachment, part,
# sticker, and recent-item trees. Filtering saves host disk space, but the
# device still sends all backup bytes during the first run. The complete
# Manifest.db is retained so later runs can use incremental backup state.
# Filtered backups are intended for data access, not full-device restore.
# Use --patch-manifest when another tool requires Manifest.db to reference
# only saved payloads. This forces each run to be full, and encrypted backups
# require --password so the manifest can be decrypted and re-encrypted.
# Filtered backups also require --patch-manifest when combined with --unback.

# Restore backup
pymobiledevice3 backup2 restore DIRECTORY

docs.title: Profiles and Configuration
docs.text:
# List installed configuration profiles
pymobiledevice3 profile list

# Install one or more profiles (.mobileconfig)
pymobiledevice3 profile install my.mobileconfig

# Remove a profile by its identifier/name
pymobiledevice3 profile remove com.example.profile

Supervised devices only: these commands escalate with the supervision identity passed as --keybag (a PEM holding the supervisor certificate and private key, e.g. from profile create-keybag).

# Save the passcode unlock token (the device must have no passcode yet); written with mode 0600
pymobiledevice3 profile request-unlock-token --keybag keybag.pem unlock-token.bin

# Later: remove the passcode without knowing it; the device then drops the pairing, so re-pair
pymobiledevice3 profile clear-passcode --keybag keybag.pem unlock-token.bin
pymobiledevice3 lockdown pair-supervised keybag.pem

# Clear the Screen Time passcode (iOS 27.2 rejects it device-side)
pymobiledevice3 profile clear-restrictions-password --keybag keybag.pem

# Security status as JSON; PasscodePresent reliably tells whether a passcode is set
pymobiledevice3 profile security-info --keybag keybag.pem

# Set the wallpaper (--screen lock|home|both; iOS 16+ may apply it to both regardless)
pymobiledevice3 profile set-wallpaper --keybag keybag.pem wallpaper.png --screen both

docs.title: Cryptexes (iOS 17+, RSD tunnel)
docs.text:
Talks to cryptexd directly. cryptex list reports a DeveloperDiskImage installed as a cryptex (by cryptex auto-install, by mounter auto-mount, or by Xcode) as com.apple.MobileAsset.DDI. A PersonalizedDMG mounted through the image mounter is not a cryptex, so it does not appear there -- mounter list shows both.

pymobiledevice3 cryptex list
pymobiledevice3 cryptex personalization-identifiers
pymobiledevice3 cryptex nonce
pymobiledevice3 cryptex nonce --nonce-domain-handle 4

State-changing. Rolling a nonce invalidates anything personalized against it, so a mounted personalized DDI must be re-personalized and re-mounted afterwards:

pymobiledevice3 cryptex roll-nonce
pymobiledevice3 cryptex uninstall com.apple.MobileAsset.DDI

cryptex auto-install is the cryptex counterpart of mounter auto-mount — a cryptex is installed, not mounted, which is why the verb differs. It personalizes and installs the DeveloperDiskImage over cryptexd alone, without the image mounter: it has Apple sign a Cryptex1 ticket for this device and installs the payloads, leaving the DDI's developer services (DVT, testmanagerd, …) usable. The end result is indistinguishable from a mounter auto-mount — mounter list reports it as a Personalized image at /System/Developer. From iOS 27, mounter auto-mount itself installs this cryptex instead of mounting the older PersonalizedDMG: unlike the PersonalizedDMG, the cryptex is not tied to the boards listed in the DDI's build manifest, so it also covers devices newer than the DDI.

iOS 26.4 and later

iOS installs the DeveloperDiskImage as a cryptex only from 26.4. Below it, cryptexd may import the image but not mount it at /System/Developer, so cryptex auto-install refuses, and mounter auto-mount mounts the PersonalizedDMG instead (#1991).

It refuses to run while a DeveloperDiskImage is already present, whichever front-end put it there: remove a cryptex with cryptex uninstall com.apple.MobileAsset.DDI, or a PersonalizedDMG with mounter umount-personalized.

Also like mounter auto-mount, it downloads the DDI it needs and caches it under ~/.pymobiledevice3 ($XDG_DATA_HOME/pymobiledevice3 on new Linux installs), so no Xcode installation is required and it works on any host:

pymobiledevice3 cryptex auto-install

# Use a local bundle instead of the download, e.g. Xcode's own
pymobiledevice3 cryptex auto-install --restore-dir /Library/Developer/DeveloperDiskImages/iOS_DDI/Restore

Overlap with mounter

cryptexd and the image mounter are two front-ends onto the same cryptex subsystem, so some queries exist in both places. Where they overlap, cryptex is the more precise source:

  • cryptex personalization-identifiers returns a strict superset of mounter query-personalization-identifiers (19 img4_chip_* fields versus 8), including the product class used by the Cryptex1,UseProductClass personalization variant.
  • cryptex nonce returns the nonce structure (56 bytes, the 48-byte nonce at offset 2); mounter query-nonce returns those 48 bytes alone.
  • cryptex nonce validates the domain and fails loudly on an unknown one, whereas mounter query-nonce silently falls back to the default nonce for an unrecognized --image-type.

mounter still wins when no tunnel can be set up: its queries work over plain USB, while every cryptex command needs RSD.

docs.title: Streaming app install
docs.text:
# Stream the app the way Xcode does: the device extracts it while it arrives,
# instead of unpacking an .ipa uploaded over AFC
pymobiledevice3 apps install --streaming MyApp.ipa
pymobiledevice3 apps install --streaming --developer build/MyApp.app

docs.title: Files in an app container (iOS 17+, RSD tunnel)
docs.text:
# Create, inspect, rename and remove files in an app's data container
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device write-file appDataContainer Documents/note.txt ./note.txt --identifier com.example.app
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device stat appDataContainer Documents/note.txt --identifier com.example.app
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device rename appDataContainer Documents/note.txt Documents/old.txt --identifier com.example.app
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device create-symlink appDataContainer Documents/latest.txt old.txt --identifier com.example.app
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device remove-file appDataContainer Documents/old.txt --identifier com.example.app

# Print changes as they happen, one JSON record per change (iOS 27+)
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device watch appDataContainer --identifier com.example.app

docs.title: App console output (iOS 17+, RSD tunnel)
docs.text:
# Launch an app and print its stdout/stderr until it exits
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device launch-application com.example.app --console

docs.title: App install records (iOS 17+)
docs.text:
# LaunchServices install record (DB UUID/sequence, install path, persistent identifier)
pymobiledevice3 apps install-record com.apple.Preferences

docs.title: Darwin Notifications
docs.text:
Darwin notifications are the system-wide named signals of notify(3), which daemons post on state changes.

# Post a notification
pymobiledevice3 notification post com.example.notification

# Subscribe and stream notifications as they fire
pymobiledevice3 notification observe com.example.notification

On iOS 17+, --remotexpc talks to the notification proxy directly over RemoteXPC instead of tunnelling the lockdown service through its .shim.remote alias. This option does not set up the tunnel by itself, so request one explicitly with --userspace (or --rsd/--tunnel):

pymobiledevice3 notification observe --remotexpc com.example.notification --userspace
pymobiledevice3 notification post --remotexpc com.example.notification --userspace

Since iOS 27.2 a notification also carries a 64-bit state, which system daemons use to publish a current value (lock state, orientation, low power mode...). Reading and setting it goes over the RSD tunnel, which the CLI sets up by itself:

# Read the current value
pymobiledevice3 notification get-state com.apple.springboard.lockstate com.apple.backboardd.orientation

# Set a value and post the notification; the device keeps the value until you hit Ctrl+C
pymobiledevice3 notification set-state com.example.notification 1

docs.title: SpringBoard UI
docs.text:
# Print current screen orientation
pymobiledevice3 springboard orientation

# Save an app's icon to a PNG
pymobiledevice3 springboard icon com.apple.mobilesafari safari-icon.png

# Save the home-screen wallpaper to a PNG
pymobiledevice3 springboard wallpaper-home-screen wallpaper.png

docs.title: Firmware Update
docs.text:
# Pick a signed build interactively, download it and update in place (keeps user data)
pymobiledevice3 restore update

# Update using a local IPSW file
pymobiledevice3 restore update -i /path/to/firmware.ipsw

# Update using an IPSW URL
pymobiledevice3 restore update -i https://example.com/firmware.ipsw

--erase restores instead, wiping the device. See the restore guide for details.

docs.title: Developer Mode and DDI
docs.text:
Developer services (everything under developer) need Developer Mode (iOS 16+). Some also need the DeveloperDiskImage (DDI), an Apple-signed image that adds developer services to the device:

  • iOS < 17: every developer service, including developer dvt, needs the DDI.
  • iOS 17+: developer dvt needs only Developer Mode. developer core-device always needs the DDI.

If a developer command fails with InvalidServiceError, mounting the DDI is the first thing to try.

# Check, then enable Developer Mode. Enabling restarts the device and only works when no passcode
# is set; otherwise reveal the switch in Settings -> Privacy & Security and turn it on there
pymobiledevice3 amfi developer-mode-status
pymobiledevice3 amfi enable-developer-mode
pymobiledevice3 amfi reveal-developer-mode

# Mount the DeveloperDiskImage (needed again after every reboot)
pymobiledevice3 mounter auto-mount

# Trust the developer app signer of an installed provisioning profile (UUID from `provision list`)
pymobiledevice3 amfi trust-app-signer PROFILE_UUID

mounter auto-mount picks the right DeveloperDiskImage for the device's iOS version:

iOS Image < 17.0 the classic DeveloperDiskImage.dmg for that version, over the image mounter 17.0 - 26.x the PersonalizedDMG over the image mounter 27.0+ the Cryptex1 DDI over cryptexd

On iOS 17+, --image cryptex|personalized-dmg overrides that choice. For example, a device whose cryptexd cannot install the cryptex (syslog live -m cryptexd shows staging failed) can still mount the PersonalizedDMG with mounter auto-mount --image personalized-dmg, as long as the DDI's build manifest lists its board.

Newer devices (e.g. the iPhone 18 series) only work with the Cryptex1 DDI

Every PersonalizedDMG build identity is tied to one chip/board pair, so it can only be personalized for the devices listed in the DDI's build manifest -- and even Xcode 27.1's DDI stops at iPhone18,5. A device outside that list gets no ticket for it (see NoSuchBuildIdentityError). The Cryptex1 identity names no device at all, so its ticket request is valid for any device and Apple's signing server decides. This is also how Xcode supports these devices, which run iOS 27 or later, where auto-mount installs the cryptex (as does cryptex auto-install).

Installing the Cryptex1 DDI needs an RSD tunnel; you don't need to pass one: the CLI sets up a no-root tunnel and retries by itself ("Trying again over ... since RSD is required for this command"). All variants are downloaded and cached under ~/.pymobiledevice3 ($XDG_DATA_HOME/pymobiledevice3 on new Linux installs), and the iOS 17+ ones end up mounted at /System/Developer. See Cryptexes for installing the cryptex directly.

docs.title: DVT Examples
docs.text:
DVT is the developer-tools service Xcode and Instruments use. These commands need Developer Mode, plus a mounted DDI on iOS < 17 (above).

# Simulate location (iOS < 17.0); `--` lets a negative coordinate through
pymobiledevice3 developer simulate-location set -- LATITUDE LONGITUDE

# Simulate location (iOS >= 17.0)
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt simulate-location set -- LATITUDE LONGITUDE

# Play GPX route
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt simulate-location play route.gpx

# Add random timing noise between -500 and 500 ms
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt simulate-location play route.gpx 500

# Clear simulated location
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt simulate-location clear

# Take a screenshot
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt screenshot /path/to/screen.png

# Detailed process list
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt sysmon process single

# Stream processes above 50% CPU
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt sysmon process monitor threshold 50

# Stream one process and only show the selected fields
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt sysmon process monitor process --filter pid=123 --key name --key cpuUsage --key physFootprint

# Stream one process with human-readable memory sizes
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt sysmon process monitor process --filter name=SpringBoard --key name --key physFootprint --human

# Keep streaming across relaunches: re-apply the filter on every snapshot instead of
# stopping once the originally selected process is gone
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt sysmon process monitor process --filter name=MyApp --choose last --keep-monitoring

# Stream oslog
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt oslog

# Stream oslog as NDJSON (one JSON object per line). Each record also carries the message's format string and its arguments
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt oslog --format json

# Kill a process
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt kill PID

# Memory of a debuggable (development-signed) app. The device refuses any other process.
# Regions of its address space
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt vm-regions PID

# Save the memory graph of a running app; prints the leak count and addresses as JSON
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt memgraph PID app.memgraph

# Inspect it with leaks(1), heap(1) or vmmap(1), which ship with macOS only
leaks app.memgraph

# To see where each allocation was made, launch the app with malloc stack logging first;
# the memory graph then carries the backtraces
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt launch --env MallocStackLogging=1 com.example.app
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt memgraph PID app.memgraph
malloc_history app.memgraph --fullStacks ADDRESS

# Launch timing, image and dlopen counts as the dynamic loader recorded them (debuggable apps only)
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt dyld-metrics PID

# Launch an app and summarize its heap allocations by class once interrupted (or after --duration)
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt allocations com.example.app --duration 10

# Print every event instead, one JSON record each, with its backtrace as image+offset frames;
# --kind adds reference-counts, vm or zombies events to the default heap ones
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt allocations com.example.app --events --kind heap --kind reference-counts

# Disable the jetsam memory limit for a process (stop it being killed for
# exceeding its memory allowance)
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt memlimitoff PID

# List files in an un-chrooted path
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt ls PATH

# Launch an app
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt launch com.apple.mobilesafari

# Live kdebug (kernel event trace) parsing, strace-like; "Tracing with kdebug" covers the details. Unfiltered, the device emits events faster than they can
# be parsed, so output fails once it falls --max-lag (2s) behind, or skips ahead (with a warning on
# stderr) with --skip-behind; --bsc / --class-filters / --subclass-filters filter on the device (by
# subclass at most). On exit it prints how many events were read, dropped by the device and
# skipped. While apps launch, --bsc keeps up over any tunnel
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt core-profile-session parse-live
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt core-profile-session parse-live --bsc

# Only some syscalls, with their paths (each also matches its _nocancel variant). The device still
# sends every syscall; the others are dropped right after decoding, which keeps up over any tunnel.
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt core-profile-session parse-live -s open -s openat

# Syscalls by subsystem: --fs (syscalls that take a path), --net (sockets), --proc (process lifecycle),
# --io (reads, writes and the other syscalls on file descriptors), --mem (memory mappings), --signal,
# --cred (credentials, code signing and policy checks, access to other tasks), --sync (locks, kqueues,
# workqueues) and --mach (Mach traps). Groups add up, and combine with -s and -e: `--fs --io` prints both.
# `events` with the same options lists exactly what is printed
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt core-profile-session parse-live --fs --io
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt core-profile-session parse-live --mem --signal --cred
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt core-profile-session events --io
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt core-profile-session events -s open

# dyld events (image loads, dlopen, dlsym, ...); unlike the syscall groups, filtered on the device
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt core-profile-session parse-live --dyld

# XPC messages and transactions, libdispatch Mach messages, CoreFoundation run loop activity, of every
# process (printed as their name and raw arguments)
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt core-profile-session parse-live --xpc --process SpringBoard
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt core-profile-session parse-live --dispatch --runloop

# Events by their trace code name (the device filters each event's subclass, and the other events
# in it are dropped right after decoding). `events TEXT` finds a name, `events` alone lists them all
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt core-profile-session events dlsym
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt core-profile-session parse-live -e DBG_DYLD_TIMING_DLOPEN -e DBG_DYLD_TIMING_DLSYM

# One JSON object per trace (time, thread, pid, process, event, parsed fields and text), e.g. for jq.
# On a terminal, traces are otherwise colored by what they show; --color-mode fast colors only the columns
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt core-profile-session parse-live --fs --json | jq -c 'select(.process == "MobileSafari")'

# Save kdebug events to a file
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt core-profile-session save FILENAME

# Print the call stacks of every thread of every process (or of one: --process PID/NAME).
# They are symbolicated using the Xcode device support of the device, which
# `developer fetch-symbols download` creates; --json prints the raw stackshot instead
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt core-profile-session stackshot --process SpringBoard

# Also symbolicate the kernel frames, given the kernelcache of the firmware the device runs
# (from its IPSW) and the `kernel` directory of https://github.com/blacktop/symbolicator.
# Requires `ipsw`; --kernelcache alone names the kernel image of each frame
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt core-profile-session stackshot \
    --kernelcache kernelcache.release.iphone17 --kernel-signatures symbolicator/kernel

# Device information
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt device-information

# Energy monitor
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt energy PID1 PID2 ...

# Per-process network traffic (bytes/packets, rx/tx)
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt network-statistics PID1 PID2 ...

# Display frame rate (Core Animation FPS), once a second
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt fps

docs.title: Core Device (iOS 17+)
docs.text:
These commands talk to iOS 17+ CoreDevice services (the ones Xcode's devicectl uses) through the RSD tunnel, which the CLI sets up by itself.

Prerequisites

These always require Developer Mode and the Developer Disk Image (DDI) mounted. Mount it once per boot with:

pymobiledevice3 mounter auto-mount

# Take a screenshot (PNG)
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device screen-capture screenshot /path/to/screen.png

# Fetch an application's icon (PNG). Size is given in points; pixel size is size * scale
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device fetch-app-icon com.apple.Preferences /path/to/icon.png
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device fetch-app-icon com.example.app /path/to/icon.png --width 176 --height 176 --scale 2

# Fail instead of returning a generic placeholder when the app has no icon
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device fetch-app-icon com.example.app /path/to/icon.png --no-placeholder

docs.title: HID input
docs.text:
# Press a named hardware button (home, lock, volume-up, volume-down, mute, siri)
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device hid button home press

# Hold/release a named button (states: down, up, canceled)
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device hid button volume-up down
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device hid button volume-up up

# Press by raw HID (usage_page, usage_code) — decimal or 0xHEX
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device hid raw-button 0x0C 0x40 press

# List the device's registered HID surfaces (each has a _ServiceID).
# Touch goes via 257 (mainTouchscreen) or 1281 (touchscreenGesture).
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device universal-hid-service list-connected

# Deliver a raw HID report to a connected surface. The layout is
# surface-specific; capture devicectl traffic with misc/remotexpc_sniffer.py
# (in a source checkout) to learn it for a new surface.
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device universal-hid-service send-report 1281 HEX_REPORT

# --- touch gestures (the media stream they need is managed automatically) ---
#
# X/Y are UInt16 (0..65535) normalised across the device's screen, so
# (0, 0) is top-left and (65535, 65535) is bottom-right regardless of the
# device's pixel resolution. Useful anchors regardless of model:
#   center                (32768, 32768)
#   top-center            (32768,  5000)
#   bottom-center         (32768, 60000)
#   home-indicator area   (32768, 62000+)
#
# On a device with several displays, the gestures go to the display in use;
# --touch-service-id picks another display's touchscreen (see list-connected).
#
# To convert from pixel coordinates, query the device's pixel size first:
#   pymobiledevice3 developer core-device get-display-info
#       # → displays[0].currentMode.size = [828, 1792] for an iPhone 11, etc.
# then scale linearly: hid_x = round(px_x * 65535 / px_w).

# Tap at the screen center
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device universal-hid-service tap -- 32768 32768

# Drag from near the top to near the bottom (e.g. pull-down)
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device universal-hid-service drag -- 32768 5000 32768 60000

# Multi-finger (up to 5): two-finger tap at X Y pairs
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device universal-hid-service multi-tap -- 26000 30000 40000 30000

# Multi-finger drag, X1 Y1 X2 Y2 (start, end) per finger: apart = zoom in,
# together = pinch, parallel = multi-finger swipe
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device universal-hid-service multi-drag -- 28000 28000 12000 20000 37536 32000 53536 40000

# Pure pointer-motion gesture (moves cursor without registering a contact)
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device universal-hid-service swipe -- 100 400 700 400

# Batched gestures inside ONE media stream — reads stdin / a script file.
# Recognised lines: tap, drag, swipe, move, sleep (and # comments).
printf 'tap 32768 32768\nsleep 0.3\ndrag 32768 5000 32768 60000\n' | \
    pymobiledevice3 developer core-device universal-hid-service session

# --- keyboard (a virtual keyboard registered for the command) ---

# Type text (a newline presses Return), then remove the last two characters
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device universal-hid-service type 'Hello'
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device universal-hid-service key backspace --count 2

docs.title: Screen streaming (HEVC video)
docs.text:
Two ways to view (and control) the device's screen live, both fed by the same device-initiated HEVC stream over the RSD tunnel. Both need iOS 27 or later: older devices never send the stream, so these commands refuse to start on them.

  • serve-web — serves the screen over HTTP for any modern browser; the HEVC decode happens in-browser via WebCodecs, so it works cross-platform with no external tools. Touch, hardware buttons (drawn on the edges of the phone frame), and keyboard are wired back to the device. The View panel zooms (Ctrl+= / Ctrl+- / Ctrl+0) and rotates the displayed device.
  • serve-vnc — serves the screen as a VNC (RFB 3.8) server for macOS Screen Sharing or any VNC client. macOS-only, because the server-side HEVC decode goes through VideoToolbox. Right-click in the viewer is the Home button; Ctrl+H/L/[/]/\/S map to Home / Lock / Volume Down / Volume Up / Mute / Siri. Add --audio to also play the device's system audio out of the host Mac's speakers.
# Query what the device's media-stream server supports
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device display get-media-support-info
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device display get-media-stream-server-status

# Serve the device screen live to any modern browser (see notes above)
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device display serve-web
# then open http://127.0.0.1:8080/

# On a device with several displays (a foldable) both show the display in use and follow a
# fold/unfold; pin one with --display-id (see get-display-info)
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device display serve-web --display-id 2

# Serve the device screen as a VNC (RFB 3.8) server, macOS-only (see notes above)
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device display serve-vnc
# then Finder ⌘K -> vnc://127.0.0.1:5901

# Either one, reachable from the rest of the LAN: bind every interface and set a password,
# since whoever reaches the port can both watch and control the device
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device display serve-web --bind 0.0.0.0 --password s3cret
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device display serve-vnc --bind 0.0.0.0 --password s3cret

# Capture raw RTP/HEVC packets to a file (length-prefixed)
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device display start-video-stream /tmp/cap.rtp --duration 10

# Convert that capture to an Annex-B .h265 bitstream playable by ffplay/VLC
# (misc/rtp_dump.py is in a source checkout, not in the installed package)
misc/rtp_dump.py /tmp/cap.rtp /tmp/cap.h265
ffplay -framerate 60 /tmp/cap.h265

Both can share the clipboard with the device, in both directions:

  • serve-web: turn on Sync in the viewer's Clipboard panel. Text and images copied on the device land in the browser machine's clipboard, and whatever was copied there is on the device by the time you paste. A picture copied out of a rich-text app such as Notes is not shared: it only exists inside the app's rich representations, and reading those blocks the device's pasteboard service for about a minute (copy the picture from Photos, or take a screenshot, instead). The browser only grants clipboard access on a secure context (localhost, or --https) and asks for permission once; it also refuses clipboard writes from a background tab, so a device copy made meanwhile lands when you return to the page.
  • serve-vnc --share-clipboard: text only (RFB has no image clipboard). Uses the RFB clipboard messages, so it follows the VNC client's own clipboard setting. UTF-8 with clients that implement the Extended Clipboard pseudo-encoding (TigerVNC, noVNC, …); other clients get the classic Latin-1 message.
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device display serve-vnc --share-clipboard

Camera and microphone conflicts

iOS will not start a screen-mirroring session while a foreground app is using the camera or microphone. This is the same restriction Apple's Xcode Device Hub enforces. If the Camera, Voice Memos, or a similar app is in the foreground when you launch serve-web / serve-vnc, the command prints a one-line explanation and exits with a non-zero code rather than serving — quit that app on the device and run it again. Conversely, while a mirroring session is active those apps cannot acquire the sensors and will record silence or black video, so stop mirroring before capturing with them.

docs.title: Location
docs.text:
# List the location-simulation scenarios baked into the device
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device location available-scenarios

docs.title: WebInspector Automation
docs.text:
# JavaScript shell on open tab (requires Web Inspector enabled: Settings -> Apps -> Safari ->
# Advanced, or Settings -> Safari -> Advanced before iOS 18)
pymobiledevice3 webinspector js-shell

# JavaScript shell filtered to one app's WebViews
pymobiledevice3 webinspector js-shell --bundle-id com.example.MyApp

# JavaScript shell without inspector console events
pymobiledevice3 webinspector js-shell --no-console-enable

# JavaScript shell without the console history the page replays on attach
pymobiledevice3 webinspector js-shell --no-replayed-log

# List opened tabs
pymobiledevice3 webinspector opened-tabs

# JavaScript shell on automation tab (requires Remote Automation enabled, next to Web Inspector)
pymobiledevice3 webinspector js-shell --automation

# JavaScript automation shell for a specific app
pymobiledevice3 webinspector js-shell --automation --bundle-id com.example.MyApp

# Launch automation session to URL
pymobiledevice3 webinspector launch URL

# Selenium-like interactive shell
pymobiledevice3 webinspector shell

# CDP bridge: debug pages with Chrome DevTools or VS Code
pymobiledevice3 webinspector cdp

See WebView debugging for the CDP bridge and the device setup in detail.

docs.title: Device Operator Skill
docs.text:
The device-operator skill teaches an AI coding agent (Claude Code or Codex) to operate a connected iPhone or iPad with pymobiledevice3. Use it when an agent needs to handle:

  • connectivity and transport selection
  • crash/log/file collection
  • app/container operations
  • DVT and other developer services
  • WebInspector and WDA automation
  • Python scripting against the library
  • thin CLI additions on top of existing services

The skill lives in this repository:

  • Skill file: .codex/skills/pymobiledevice3-device-operator/SKILL.md
  • Reference file: .codex/skills/pymobiledevice3-device-operator/references/quick-recipes.md
  • Reference file: .codex/skills/pymobiledevice3-device-operator/references/python-scripting.md
  • Reference file: .codex/skills/pymobiledevice3-device-operator/references/task-map.md
  • Reference file: .codex/skills/pymobiledevice3-device-operator/references/transport-and-safety.md

Inside a checkout, the skill is discovered automatically by both Codex (via .codex/skills/) and Claude Code (via a symlink in .claude/skills/). The two skill trees mirror each other with relative symlinks; see Skills in the agent guidance for the full inventory and the edit-the-canonical-copy convention.

docs.title: Install Into Your Own Claude Code
docs.text:
You do not need to work inside this repository to use the skill. The commands it teaches run against the PyPI release via uvx pymobiledevice3 ..., so a fresh workstation only needs uv and a USB-connected device. Without uv, the skill falls back to a plain pip install and can also install uv without root.

As a plugin (recommended). This repository doubles as a Claude Code plugin marketplace. Inside Claude Code run:

/plugin marketplace add doronz88/pymobiledevice3
/plugin install pymobiledevice3-device-operator@pymobiledevice3

After installing, Claude can take screenshots, search the device syslog, pull crash reports, manage apps and files, and drive developer services from any directory.

As a personal skill (manual). Clone the repository once and symlink the skill into your personal skills directory:

git clone https://github.com/doronz88/pymobiledevice3.git
mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills
ln -s "$(pwd)/pymobiledevice3/.codex/skills/pymobiledevice3-device-operator" ~/.claude/skills/

docs.title: What The Skill Enforces
docs.text:
• Prefer existing CLI commands and service modules over new abstractions.
  • Prefer uvx --from . pymobiledevice3 ... inside a local checkout, and uvx pymobiledevice3 ... without one.
  • Prefer reading local docs and CLI source before invoking --help.
  • Treat --help as a fallback or final verification step.
  • Require explicit user intent before state-changing or destructive device actions.
  • Check transport, developer-mode, image-mount, and tunnel prerequisites before assuming a code bug.

docs.title: Transport Notes
docs.text:
For iOS 17+ developer services, the skill routes users through the project tunnel documentation and transport rules in:

  • iOS 17+ tunnels
  • .codex/skills/pymobiledevice3-device-operator/references/transport-and-safety.md

On iOS 17.4+ no tunnel setup is needed at all: commands that require an RSD tunnel establish a no-root in-process userspace tunnel automatically, so the skill routes agents straight to the target command. On macOS, iOS 17.0-17.3 devices fall back to the no-root --native tunnel. Privileged tunnels (tunneld, start-tunnel) remain the fallback for iOS 17.0-17.3 devices on Linux/Windows, or when the no-root paths are not viable (e.g. a tunnel shared across processes or reachable by external tools).

For agent-driven start-tunnel startup on those fallback paths, the skill prefers lockdown start-tunnel --script-mode or remote start-tunnel --script-mode (with sudo if tunnel interface creation needs elevated privileges), then reads the RSD connection details from stdout and feeds those exact values into later --rsd HOST PORT commands.

docs.title: When Updating The Project
docs.text:
If you add, remove, or substantially change device-facing CLI behavior, update the skill guidance when needed so agents keep routing requests correctly.

In practice, review the skill when changes affect:

  • top-level or nested CLI command layout
  • transport selection (USB, --rsd, --tunnel)
  • iOS version-specific command routing
  • safety expectations for state-changing commands
  • preferred service module or CLI entry point for a task

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
Every pymobiledevice3 environment variable, what it sets, and where it is explained in depth. Each one is a default: where a matching command-line option exists, the option always wins.

Set a variable for the current shell session like this:

macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
export PYMOBILEDEVICE3_UDID=00008110-001234567890801E

$env:PYMOBILEDEVICE3_UDID = "00008110-001234567890801E"

pymobiledevice3 usbmux list shows each connected device's UDID (its unique device identifier).

docs.title: Device selection
docs.text: Variable Value Effect PYMOBILEDEVICE3_UDID device UDID Default for --udid — the device every command targets. PYMOBILEDEVICE3_RECONNECT_ANY any non-empty value With --reconnect: after a mid-command disconnect, reconnect to the first available device even when its UDID differs from the device the command originally targeted. A warning is printed and the re-invocation targets the newly connected device. PYMOBILEDEVICE3_USBMUX unix socket path or HOST:PORT Default for --usbmux — where usbmuxd is listening. USBMUXD_SOCKET_ADDRESS unix socket path or HOST:PORT Same as above; honored for compatibility with libimobiledevice.

docs.title: Transport (iOS 17+ tunnels)
docs.text:
Variable Value Effect PYMOBILEDEVICE3_DEFAULT_FALLBACK native, userspace or tunneld Which transport the automatic selection prefers, both for commands that require an RSD and for the retry the CLI performs when a command turns out to need a tunnel. Built-in default: userspace. An unrecognized value logs a warning and is ignored. PYMOBILEDEVICE3_NATIVE 1 Same as --native: piggyback Apple's remoted tunnel via remotepairingd. macOS only, no root, opt-in (see Native remoted tunnel). PYMOBILEDEVICE3_USERSPACE 1 Same as --userspace: force the in-process pure-Python userspace tunnel. PYMOBILEDEVICE3_TUNNEL UDID, UDID:PORT or UDID@HOST[:PORT] Same as --tunnel: take the tunnel from a running tunneld; the @HOST form bridges through a remote tunneld's WS /connect. An empty UDID picks the only tunnel, or prompts.

--rsd, --tunnel, --userspace and --native are mutually exclusive, so set at most one of their variables. See iOS 17+ tunnels for when each transport applies, and Understanding the network stacks for how they differ.

# prefer the macOS native tunnel for this shell
export PYMOBILEDEVICE3_DEFAULT_FALLBACK=native

docs.title: Restore and Recovery/DFU
docs.text: Variable Value Effect PYMOBILEDEVICE3_IPSW_DIR directory Default for --ipsw-dir on the restore commands that take an IPSW: reuse a firmware build already downloaded there, and download new ones into it instead of a temporary directory. PYMOBILEDEVICE3_USB_BACKEND iokit or libusb Same as restore --libusb when set to libusb: reach Recovery/DFU devices through libusb instead of IOKit on macOS. iokit is only valid on macOS; other platforms always use libusb.

docs.title: Output
docs.text: Variable Value Effect NO_COLOR any non-empty value Disables colored output and logs, like --no-color (see no-color.org).

docs.title: Advanced
docs.text: Variable Value Effect PYMOBILEDEVICE3_NATIVE_TARGET_UID numeric uid Which login user's remotepairingd the native tunnel talks to. remotepairingd is registered per-user, so a root process (CI runner, LaunchDaemon) needs this to reach the pairing owned by the logged-in user. Ignored (with a warning) when not running as root.

docs.title: Set by your environment, not by you
docs.text:
These are read from the environment your shell or OS already provides; they are listed so their effect is not a surprise.

Variable Effect SUDO_USER Under sudo, pymobiledevice3 resolves ~ (and therefore ~/.pymobiledevice3 — or $XDG_DATA_HOME/pymobiledevice3 on new Linux installs — where pair records live) to the invoking user's home, not root's. SUDO_UID, SUDO_GID Files pymobiledevice3 creates under sudo are chowned back to the invoking user, so a later non-root run can still read them. XDG_DATA_HOME Linux only: fresh installations keep pymobiledevice3's files under $XDG_DATA_HOME/pymobiledevice3 (~/.local/share/pymobiledevice3 when unset), per the XDG Base Directory Specification. An existing ~/.pymobiledevice3 keeps being used. Note that plain sudo (env_reset) strips this variable, so a sudo run falls back to ~/.local/share of the invoking user — use sudo -E (or env_keep) if your XDG_DATA_HOME points elsewhere and the sudo run should match. ALLUSERSPROFILE Windows only: where Apple's Lockdown pair records are looked up (%ALLUSERSPROFILE%\Apple\Lockdown). TERM Passed through to the shell developer debugserver spawns; defaults to xterm-256color. _PYMOBILEDEVICE3_COMPLETE Set by the shell-completion scripts (--install-completion). Its presence makes commands skip connecting to the device.

docs.title: iOS 17+ Developer Services via Tunnel
docs.text:
Starting with iOS 17.0, Apple moved the developer services (the ones Xcode uses: process lists, screenshots, location simulation, debugging, ...) behind an encrypted tunnel to the device. Inside that tunnel, an index service called RSD (RemoteServiceDiscovery) lists the services, which speak Apple's RemoteXPC protocol. So developer commands (and a few others) need such a tunnel.

You usually don't need to do anything. pymobiledevice3 establishes the tunnel for you, in-process, with no root/admin and no extra software. Just run the command:

pymobiledevice3 developer dvt ls /

On iOS 17.4 and later this works the same on macOS, Windows and Linux. The rest of this page is advanced material: you need it only for iOS 17.0-17.3 on Linux/Windows, for external tools such as lldb, or for a tunnel shared between many commands (see When you still need tunneld).

Working from Python?

See Choosing a connection in the Python API guide for when to use lockdown vs an RSD tunnel (userspace vs tunneld).

Reference protocol details: RemoteXPC

Tip

For diagrams of what each transport path looks like under the hood — usbmux, Wi-Fi lockdown, kernel tunnels, the userspace tunnel and the macOS native tunnel — see Understanding the network stacks.

docs.title: The default: a no-root tunnel, automatically
docs.text:
When a developer command needs an RSD tunnel and you passed no transport flag (--rsd / --tunnel / --userspace / --native), pymobiledevice3 brings up a no-root tunnel for you, built when the command starts and torn down when it exits: an in-process userspace tunnel using a pure-Python network stack (PyTCP) — no kernel interface, so no root/admin either, on every host.

This covers iOS 17.4+ over USB (it uses the device's CoreDeviceProxy lockdown service) and is the right choice almost every time. When you do need more throughput or lower latency than the userspace stack gives, use a kernel-routable tunnel (one the operating system can route to, so any process can reach it). On macOS the opt-in --native transport, which rides Apple's own remoted tunnel, is the fastest and needs no root, but it is less stable because it competes with remoted for the device; see Native remoted tunnel. Otherwise use a privileged tunneld (below).

iOS 17.0-17.3 devices, which the userspace tunnel cannot serve, are routed automatically to the native tunnel on macOS and to tunneld elsewhere; see the warning below. Set PYMOBILEDEVICE3_DEFAULT_FALLBACK=native|userspace|tunneld to change which transport the automatic selection prefers (see Environment variables for every variable the CLI honors).

iOS 17.0-17.3 needs tunneld on Linux/Windows

These versions predate the CoreDeviceProxy service, so the userspace tunnel can only reach them over the RemotePairing path — which is Wi-Fi-only and, on macOS, races remoted (the no-root path can't suspend it without root). Rather than depend on that fragile path, pymobiledevice3 routes iOS 17.0-17.3 to the native tunnel on macOS (still no root — remoted already reaches these devices) and to tunneld on Linux/Windows, so keep one running there (on Windows, without sudo, from an Administrator terminal):

sudo pymobiledevice3 remote tunneld

On Linux, sudo may not find a per-user install; see Running with sudo.

You can still force the userspace path with --userspace where it applies (a device on Wi-Fi; unreliable on macOS).

docs.title: Support Notes
docs.text: Host OS iOS 17.0-17.3 iOS 17.4+ macOS Supported (no root, native tunnel) Supported (no root) Windows Needs tunneld (Administrator) + a third-party driver (see below) Supported (no root) Linux Needs tunneld (root) Supported (no root)

docs.title: When you still need a privileged tunneld
docs.text:
Advanced. tunneld is a long-running pymobiledevice3 daemon that keeps a kernel tunnel to each connected device and hands it to any command that asks (--tunnel). Creating the kernel network interface is what needs root/Administrator.

The in-process tunnel's device address lives only inside the pymobiledevice3 process, so it is not reachable from any other process on your machine. Use a kernel-routable tunnel (the sections below) when:

  • An external tool must reach the device — developer debugserver lldb, or developer debugserver start-server without --local-port, drive an external lldb and therefore refuse over the userspace tunnel. Pass --tunnel (or --native on macOS, or --local-port for start-server, which forwards to a local port and does work over the userspace tunnel).
  • You want one shared/persistent tunnel reused across many invocations instead of rebuilding it per command.
  • You need more performance than the userspace stack gives, such as bulk transfers. On macOS, --native is faster still but less stable (see above).
  • iOS 17.0-17.3 on Linux/Windows — routed to tunneld automatically; see the warning above.

docs.title: Running tunneld
docs.text:
# If the device supports remote pairing (for example, Corellium/Apple TV/Apple Vision Pro), pair first.
# Apple TV and Apple Vision Pro display a PIN to type in. Standard iOS devices usually do not need this step.
pymobiledevice3 remote pair

# On Windows, drop `sudo` and run from an Administrator terminal.
sudo pymobiledevice3 remote tunneld

With tunneld running, point a command at it with --tunnel (empty value = pick automatically, or pass a UDID):

pymobiledevice3 developer dvt ls / --tunnel ''

tunneld binds 127.0.0.1:49151 by default. To relocate it, pass --host/--port; the --tunnel value accepts the matching UDID:PORT suffix (the UDID part may be empty).

When the client cannot reach the tunnel interface tunneld created — for example, tunneld runs in a different docker network stack, or on a different host altogether — the RSD addresses reported over GET / are unreachable. The /connect websocket endpoint bridges into the tunnel through the HTTP API instead: binary websocket messages are forwarded as-is over a TCP connection opened on the device's tunnel address (to ?port=, defaulting to the RSD port), and vice versa:

import websockets  # any websocket client works

async with websockets.connect(f'ws://127.0.0.1:49151/connect?udid={udid}') as websocket:
    # speak RSD (RemoteXPC) over the websocket, or pass ?port=<service-port>
    # to reach any other service published over the tunnel
    ...

pymobiledevice3 itself consumes this bridge through the --tunnel UDID@HOST[:PORT] form (IPv6 in brackets), so every command works against a remote tunneld without any extra tooling:

# on the machine with the device attached
sudo pymobiledevice3 remote tunneld --host 0.0.0.0

# anywhere that can reach it
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt ls / --tunnel 'UDID@lab-mac:49151'

Library consumers get the same via get_tunneld_devices(('lab-mac', 49151)) / get_tunneld_device_by_udid(...) — connections are bridged automatically whenever the tunneld host is non-loopback, and the bridge=True parameter forces it for addresses that only look local (e.g. an SSH port-forward such as ssh -L 49151:127.0.0.1:49151 lab-mac, where the @ form does the same on the CLI: --tunnel UDID@127.0.0.1).

Warning

Like the rest of the tunneld HTTP API, /connect is unauthenticated — anyone able to reach the listener gains access to the services exposed over the tunnel, so only bind non-loopback addresses on trusted networks.

docs.title: Fronting several hosts with one tunneld
docs.text:
A tunneld can federate others with --upstream (repeatable, also POST /upstream at runtime). Their devices appear in its GET / listing, and a /connect for a device it does not serve itself is relayed to the upstream that owns it — so a client needs a route to the front tunneld alone, with no VPN and no route to each host's tunnel interface:

# on every host with devices attached
sudo pymobiledevice3 remote tunneld --host 0.0.0.0

# on the one host clients can reach. Disable the monitors if devices are attached here too,
# unless you want this instance to serve them itself: otherwise it builds its own tunnels
# alongside the ones it federates, and each such device is then listed twice
sudo pymobiledevice3 remote tunneld --host 0.0.0.0 \
    --no-usb --no-wifi --no-usbmux --no-mobdev2 \
    --upstream http://lab-1:49151 --upstream http://lab-2:49151

# from anywhere: any device in the lab, addressed through the front tunneld
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt ls / --tunnel 'UDID@front:49151'

Upstreams are addressed as HOST, HOST:PORT or http://HOST[:PORT] (IPv6 in brackets), all stored canonically as http://HOST:PORT with tunneld's default port filled in. https:// is rejected: the relay speaks plaintext, so carry federation over a trusted network or an SSH forward.

Each listing entry carries an origin: null for devices the queried instance serves directly, otherwise the URL of the upstream it came from. A client that can reach that upstream may skip the relay and address it directly, which saves a hop.

Note

Federated requests carry a hop budget (x-tunneld-hops-remaining, 4 by default), so tunnelds registering each other terminate instead of recursing, and a device reachable through several paths is listed once. Relaying costs an extra hop through the front instance's event loop — negligible for control traffic, measurable on bulk transfers such as DDI mounts.

To make tunneld the default fallback — so commands route to it automatically without passing --tunnel, restoring the pre-userspace-default behavior — set PYMOBILEDEVICE3_DEFAULT_FALLBACK=tunneld:

export PYMOBILEDEVICE3_DEFAULT_FALLBACK=tunneld
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt ls /

docs.title: Starting a tunnel manually
docs.text:
You rarely need this: pymobiledevice3 commands build their own tunnel. Start one by hand only for the cases in When you still need a privileged tunneld, and if you need it for more than one command, prefer running tunneld. A manual tunnel prints an --rsd HOST PORT option to pass to later commands.

# Optional for remote-pairing devices.
pymobiledevice3 remote pair

# iOS 17.4+ (lockdown tunnel, over USB)
sudo pymobiledevice3 lockdown start-tunnel

# Optional: allow Wi-Fi connections over lockdown
pymobiledevice3 lockdown wifi-connections on

# RemotePairing tunnel: the only manual option for iOS 17.0-17.3.
# Add `-t wifi` to tunnel over Wi-Fi instead of USB.
sudo pymobiledevice3 remote start-tunnel

# macOS, no sudo: publishes Apple's own remoted tunnel instead of creating one.
# It competes with remoted for the device; see "Native remoted tunnel" in the
# network stacks guide.
pymobiledevice3 remote start-tunnel --native

Example output:

Interface: utun6
RSD Address: fd7b:e5b:6f53::1
RSD Port: 64337
Use the following connection option:
--rsd fd7b:e5b:6f53::1 64337

The classic tunnel creation command must run with elevated privileges because it creates a virtual network interface (a TUN device, shown as utunN on macOS). The native path (--native, macOS) is the exception: it rides Apple's already-existing tunnel instead of creating one, so it needs no privileges. Device selection there is by --udid; the classic-tunnel-shaping options (--protocol/--secrets/--max-idle-timeout/ -t) don't apply to it, and passing one routes the command to the classic tunnel. Without --native (or PYMOBILEDEVICE3_DEFAULT_FALLBACK=native) the command builds the classic tunnel. remote browse is different: on macOS it lists devices via remotepairingd with no root by default, since browsing opens no RSD connection (--no-native forces the bonjour browse, which needs root to suspend remoted).

Bootstrap the RemotePairing record over USB (no Trust dialog)

remote start-tunnel (the RSD/Wi-Fi path) needs a RemotePairing pair record. You can create it over USB, promptlessly, via the com.apple.dt.remotepairingdeviced.lockdown control channel:

pymobiledevice3 lockdown remotepairing --pair

Because this runs over the already-trusted lockdownd (USB) transport, pairing is promptless (no on-device Trust dialog) and writes the same pair record remote start-tunnel / remote pair use. Without --pair the command just performs a handshake and prints the device's control-channel info (add --raw to keep the deviceKVSData blob base64-encoded). This control channel does not create tunnels itself.

Wi-Fi discovery needs a pair record created by a recent version

A device advertising RemotePairing over Wi-Fi is recognized by matching its bonjour authTag against the altIRK the device hands over during pairing, so only devices you are paired with are ever contacted. Pair records written before that key was stored cannot be matched: a warning names the stale remote_<udid>.plist; delete it and pair again (the promptless USB command above is the easiest way). See RemoteXPC: Wi-Fi for how the matching works.

docs.title: Forcing the userspace tunnel (--userspace)
docs.text:
The userspace tunnel is already the default, so you rarely need the flag. Pass --userspace explicitly to force the no-root in-process tunnel and skip the automatic native/tunneld fallback (iOS 17.0-17.3) — any establishment failure is then surfaced as an error rather than masked:

pymobiledevice3 developer dvt ls / --userspace

Requirements:

  • Nothing to install: the pmd-pytcp network stack behind it is a regular dependency.
  • iOS 17.4+ over USB (through the CoreDeviceProxy lockdown service), or iOS 17.0-17.3 on Wi-Fi (through RemotePairing, discovered over bonjour).

What works over the userspace tunnel: the host-initiated developer services (dvt, fetch-symbols, core-device …), and the device-initiated AV/HID paths — display serve-web, display serve-vnc, display start-video-stream / start-audio-stream, and the HID gesture commands.

Service connections are handed off in-process over a socketpair() per connection, so there is no listener another process could connect to.

docs.title: Limitation: in-process only
docs.text:
The device's tunnel address lives only inside the pymobiledevice3 process, so it is not reachable from any other process on your machine. Commands that hand the device address to an external tool therefore cannot use the userspace tunnel — see When you still need tunneld.

Because the tunnel is rebuilt per invocation (no persistent daemon), expect a little extra startup latency compared with attaching to an already-running tunneld.

docs.title: From Python
docs.text: To establish this tunnel programmatically, use the UserspaceRsdTunnel handle — see the UserspaceRsdTunnel example in the protocol-layers guide, listed there alongside the other ways to obtain an RSD. The in-process-only limitation above applies equally to the Python API.

docs.title: Use tunnel details in commands
docs.text:
# Default: no flag, no root — an in-process userspace tunnel is established automatically
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt ls /

# Force the no-root tunnel (skip the automatic tunneld fallback)
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt ls / --userspace

# Use a running tunneld ('' = pick automatically, or pass a UDID)
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt ls / --tunnel ''

# Use manual RSD connection details (from `start-tunnel`)
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt ls / --rsd fd7b:e5b:6f53::1 64337

# Non-developer command over a running tunneld
pymobiledevice3 syslog live --tunnel ''

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Most developer commands need no flag — the no-root tunnel is established for you. If one fails to establish a tunnel, the two explicit routes are --tunnel '' (uses a running tunneld) or --userspace (forces the no-root in-process tunnel and surfaces the real error).
  • iOS 17.0-17.3 is routed to the native tunnel on macOS and to tunneld on Linux/Windows (the userspace path only reaches those over the fragile Wi-Fi RemotePairing route), so start tunneld there. --userspace can still force the userspace path over Wi-Fi if you prefer.
  • Make sure the device is unlocked and trusts this computer; if you use tunneld or a manual tunnel, make sure it is still running.
  • On Windows, iOS 17.0-17.3 needs a third-party driver that pymobiledevice3 does not ship or endorse. Update the device to iOS 17.4 or later instead: it then works on Windows with no driver and no Administrator.
  • Wi-Fi-only usage (no USB cable): run pymobiledevice3 lockdown wifi-connections on once over USB. After that the host's own daemon finds the device over Wi-Fi and every command keeps working with no extra flag — on macOS always, and on Windows when the Apple Mobile Device Service comes from the classic iTunes installer. If pymobiledevice3 usbmux list stays empty while the device is on the same network, the daemon has no network-device support. On Windows that means the Microsoft Store "Apple Devices" app, whose service discovers nothing over Wi-Fi (its own UI cannot reach the device either) — install iTunes from https://www.apple.com/itunes/download/win64 instead, which is the real fix and needs no flags afterwards. On Linux, stock libimobiledevice usbmuxd has the same gap, with no equivalent daemon to switch to. Where the daemon cannot be fixed, check the device is advertising with pymobiledevice3 bonjour mobdev2 and ask for bonjour discovery explicitly with --mobdev2, which reaches it over the regular lockdown pair record on TCP — no RemotePairing record needed. Discovery is never implicit: a device usbmuxd cannot see fails immediately rather than every miss paying for a network browse, and nothing is ever served from a device you did not name.

docs.title: Tracing Syscalls and Kernel Events (kdebug)
docs.text:
