kdebug is the kernel's event tracing facility: the kernel and many system libraries record fixed-size events into it, and a trace session collects them from every process at once. It needs no entitlement, no jailbreak and no change to the traced processes, so it is the main way to watch what platform binaries (daemons, SpringBoard, Apple's apps) do on a stock device.

pymobiledevice3 developer dvt core-profile-session drives the same trace sessions as Instruments. Like every DVT command it needs Developer Mode, plus a mounted DeveloperDiskImage on iOS < 17 (see Developer Mode and DDI); on iOS 17+ the CLI sets up the tunnel by itself. CLI recipes lists more examples; this guide covers what is in a trace and how to get at it.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: Command Prints parse-live Decoded traces (strace-like): syscalls with their arguments and paths, dyld image loads, process and thread lifecycle. Selects events by group and name (--fs, --xpc, -s, -e, ...; see below). live Every raw event: time, event name, start/end, thread, process and the four raw arguments. Selects events by class and subclass. callstacks-live User space call stacks sampled from the running threads. save The raw trace, to parse later. stackshot The call stacks of every thread of every process, once.

docs.title: Event ids
docs.text:
Every event is a 32-bit debugid:

| class (8) | subclass (8) | code (14) | function (2) |

The class names the component (0x04 BSD, 0x29 XPC, ...), the subclass a part of it, and the function bits mark whether the event starts (1) or ends (2) an interval. The eventid is the debugid without the function bits, and is what trace codes name (0x29000044 is XPC_connection_send_message).

live filters on the device by class (-cf 0x29) and by class and subclass together (-sf 0x0301, the class in the high byte), which also keeps the device from sending what is filtered out:

# XPC and libdispatch events of every process
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt core-profile-session live -cf 0x29 -cf 0x2e

# file lookups only (VFS_LOOKUP lives in class 0x03, subclass 0x01)
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt core-profile-session live -sf 0x0301

docs.title: Selecting events in parse-live
docs.text:
Option Selects --fs, --net, --proc, --io, --mem, --signal, --cred, --sync, --mach A group of syscalls and Mach traps --dyld dyld image loads and timing (dlopen, dlsym, ...) --xpc, --dispatch, --runloop The XPC, libdispatch and CoreFoundation run loop events of every process, printed as their name and raw arguments -s NAME One syscall, with its _nocancel variant (-s open) -e NAME One event, by its trace code name (-e DBG_DYLD_TIMING_DLSYM)

They all add up, and --process narrows the result to one process. The device filters by subclass at best, so the host drops the rest right after decoding. events takes the same options and lists exactly the events parse-live prints with them (events --fs, events -s open), and events dlsym finds a name by text. A class or subclass filter (--bsc, -cf, -sf, --dyld) prints only the events pykdebugparser (the library that decodes the trace) knows: events -cf 0x29 lists nothing, while --xpc selects the same XPC events by id.

# the XPC traffic of SpringBoard
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt core-profile-session parse-live --xpc --process SpringBoard

# every dlsym, in every process
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt core-profile-session events dlsym
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt core-profile-session parse-live -e DBG_DYLD_TIMING_DLSYM

docs.title: Events every process emits
docs.text:
These are recorded by the kernel or by system libraries in every process, gated only by the trace session's class filter. They were all seen in traces of an iPhone on iOS 27.2.

Class Source Events What they show 0x03 kernel VFS_LOOKUP The full path of every file lookup, in every process 0x04 kernel BSD syscalls Every syscall with its arguments (parse-live decodes them) 0x07 kernel thread and process lifecycle New threads, execs and thread names 0x1f dyld image map (DYLD_uuid_map_a/b) and timing The UUID and load address of every image of every process, and dyld's launch phases 0x29 libxpc XPC_* Messages sent and received, transactions, the process becoming dirty or clean 0x2e libdispatch DISPATCH_MACH_MSG_hdr_move, DISPATCH_PERF_* Mach messages received through dispatch, queue misuse 0x21, 0x14 CoreFoundation CFRL_* Run loop iterations, waits, sources, timers, observers and blocks

The XPC events carry a per-connection id and the message size (on the end of a send), not the service name. The run loop events show when a main thread is busy and with what kind of callout, which helps find hangs.

callstacks-live samples user space call stacks of the same processes. It prints them as raw addresses; the dyld image map above tells which image each one falls in.

docs.title: Events that need a setting
docs.text:
Some system libraries emit events only when a setting enables them, on top of the trace's class filter.

Class Source Enabled by 0x33 libsystem_malloc: every malloc, calloc, realloc, free (zone, size, pointer) The MallocTracing environment variable, read when the process starts 0x2b (subclasses 0x1d, 0x13, 0x29) Network.framework, libquic, CFNetwork and BoringSSL: connections, TLS handshakes, QUIC packet protection networkd's enable_signposts setting, which only networkd's privileged clients can set

MallocTracing can be passed to apps, including Apple's own, by launching them through pymobiledevice3:

pymobiledevice3 developer dvt launch --kill-existing --env MallocTracing=1 com.apple.Preferences
pymobiledevice3 developer dvt core-profile-session live -cf 0x33

Launching only works for apps. Daemons and SpringBoard are started by launchd with launchd's environment, so there is no way to pass them MallocTracing on a stock device. CoreDevice can spawn arbitrary executables with an environment, but only on Apple internal builds.

docs.title: What kdebug does not show
docs.text:
• Mach message send and receive in the kernel (MACH_IPC_msg_send/_recv): the iOS 27.2 release kernel does not emit them. The XPC and libdispatch events cover most of that traffic from user space.
  • Message contents, XPC service names and TLS plaintext: no event carries them.

docs.title: Machine-readable output
docs.text: Most query-style pymobiledevice3 commands print JSON on stdout, ready for jq or any JSON parser. This page documents the conventions that output follows so scripts can rely on them.

docs.title: Streams
docs.text:
• stdout carries data. JSON documents, NDJSON records, and text-mode data lines all go to stdout.
  • stderr carries diagnostics. Logging, progress, and warnings never mix into the data stream. Redirect stderr away (2>/dev/null, or 2>$null in PowerShell) without losing any data.

docs.title: Binary values
docs.text:
JSON has no binary type. Values that are bytes on the device (nonces, digests, keys, certificates) are encoded as a single-key object tagged $hex:

{
    "ApNonce": {
        "$hex": "a1b2c3d4"
    }
}

Decode with bytes.fromhex in Python, or in jq keep the hex string with .ApNonce["$hex"]. A $hex object never has additional keys, so isinstance(value, dict) and value.keys() == {"$hex"} is a reliable detector when round-tripping arbitrary output:

def decode(obj):
    if isinstance(obj, dict):
        if obj.keys() == {"$hex"}:
            return bytes.fromhex(obj["$hex"])
        return {k: decode(v) for k, v in obj.items()}
    if isinstance(obj, list):
        return [decode(v) for v in obj]
    return obj

docs.title: Timestamps
docs.text: Datetimes are ISO 8601 (datetime.isoformat()), e.g. 2026-08-08T12:00:00+03:00. Values without an explicit timezone are naive device- or host-local times.

docs.title: Streaming commands: NDJSON
docs.text:
Streaming commands print one compact JSON object per line (NDJSON) on stdout — nothing else is written to stdout, so the stream can be piped directly:

pymobiledevice3 syslog live --format json -m kernel | jq .message
pymobiledevice3 diagnostics battery monitor | jq .CurrentCapacity

Streams whose records are structured data emit NDJSON always:

  • developer dvt graphics
  • developer dvt fps
  • developer dvt energy
  • developer dvt network-statistics
  • developer dvt notifications
  • developer dvt sysmon process monitor threshold / developer dvt sysmon process monitor process (optionally to a file via --output)
  • diagnostics battery monitor
  • notification observe / notification observe-all

Streams that also have a human-readable text rendering default to it and accept --format json:

  • syslog live
  • developer dvt oslog
  • developer dvt netstat
  • developer accessibility notifications
  • crash watch

docs.title: Understanding the network stacks
docs.text:
Every pymobiledevice3 command reaches the device through one of five transport paths. This guide shows what each path actually looks like — which sockets exist, what needs root, and how a device disconnect is detected.

Background reading

You don't need this page to use pymobiledevice3: commands pick the right path on their own. For choosing between paths day-to-day, see iOS 17+ tunnels.

A few terms used throughout: usbmuxd is the host daemon (part of iTunes/Apple Devices on Windows, built into macOS, a separate package on Linux) that multiplexes connections to USB devices; lockdownd is the device daemon that pairs with hosts and starts services; RSD (RemoteServiceDiscovery) is the service index that iOS 17+ exposes inside an encrypted tunnel.

docs.title: USB lockdown via usbmuxd
docs.text:
The classic path, used by everything that does not need an RSD tunnel (afc, backup2, syslog, apps, ...) and the one most commands take. No TCP on the host at all: the client speaks the usbmux protocol over usbmuxd's unix socket, and usbmuxd multiplexes device-port streams over the USB link.

flowchart LR
    cli["pymobiledevice3"] -->|"/var/run/usbmuxd<br/>(unix socket)"| mux["usbmuxd"]
    mux -->|USB| dev["iOS device<br/>lockdownd + services"]
  • Root: not required.
  • Disconnect: usbmuxd owns the link — on unplug it closes your socket immediately (kernel EOF, no probing needed).
  • On Windows usbmuxd's socket is loopback TCP (127.0.0.1:27015) instead of a unix socket.

docs.title: Wi-Fi lockdown (mobdev2)
docs.text:
The same lockdown protocol, carried over the LAN to port 62078 (--mobdev2 / get_mobdev2_lockdowns). Devices are discovered over bonjour.

flowchart LR
    cli["pymobiledevice3"] -->|"TCP :62078 over Wi-Fi"| dev["iOS device<br/>lockdownd + services"]
  • Root: not required.
  • Disconnect: a Wi-Fi link can die silently, so these connections run TCP keep-alive (idle 3 s / interval 3 s) — a vanished device errors out within seconds.

docs.title: Kernel tunnel (start-tunnel / tunneld)
docs.text:
iOS 17+ developer services live behind an encrypted tunnel to an RSD endpoint. The kernel tunnel terminates that tunnel in a kernel TUN interface (utunN on macOS; this section uses the macOS name), making the device's tunnel address (fdxx::1) kernel-routable — reachable by any process, including external tools like lldb.

flowchart LR
    subgraph host["host (root required)"]
        cli["pymobiledevice3<br/>(or any tool)"]
        utun["utunX<br/>fdxx::/64"]
        td["start-tunnel / tunneld"]
    end
    cli -->|"kernel TCP6 to [fdxx::1]"| utun
    utun --> td
    td -->|"encrypted tunnel over<br/>USB (CoreDeviceProxy) or Wi-Fi"| dev["iOS device<br/>RSD + services"]
  • Root: required (creating utun needs it); tunneld is the daemon form that shares tunnels across processes, queryable over HTTP (--tunnel).
  • Disconnect: the utun interface disappears with the tunnel, erroring connections out; service connections also run TCP keep-alive.
  • Highest host→device throughput; together with the native tunnel (macOS), the only path external tools can use.

docs.title: Why this path suspends remoted on macOS (and why that needs root)
docs.text:
Root is needed here for two independent reasons. The obvious one is creating the utun. The second is remoted contention, and it is worth spelling out because it is easy to misdiagnose.

Discovery on this path is bonjour plus a direct RSD connection: get_rsds() browses _remoted._tcp and then opens the device's RSD RemoteXPC endpoint (port 58783) on the USB NCM link (fe80::…%enX). macOS remoted owns that link — it keeps its own RemoteXPC session to the device open at all times (lsof shows an ESTABLISHED …->[fe80::…]:58783). While remoted is running, the device resets a second, independent RSD root channel opened by pymobiledevice3 — seen as an HTTP/2 RST_STREAM with error_code=5, or a plain connection reset, during the check-in handshake. So discovery finds the device but yields no usable RSD.

stop_remoted() SIGSTOPs remoted for the duration of the handshake and resumes it afterwards; suspending a root-owned daemon is what needs root. With remoted suspended the handshake succeeds reliably, and the device will even accept several concurrent RSD sessions — which shows the reset is caused by remoted owning the link, not by any device-side one-session cap.

This is not a pairing problem. A long-standing assumption held that the device closes the host's RSD fd during pairing, forcing remoted to race us — hence sudo. That is not what happens. The contention reproduces against an already-paired device with no pairing in flight, and completing a pairing does not tear down existing RSD connections (the device simply adds the new tunnel endpoint; remotepairingdeviced logs no control-channel teardown). The trigger is only that remoted is an always-on RSD client for the NCM link. Verified empirically on iPhone18,4 / iOS 26.6.1, and against the iOS 17.0, 26.6 and 27 device daemons.

The no-root userspace tunnel sidesteps all of this: it reaches RSD through the CoreDeviceProxy lockdown service over usbmux, never touching the NCM link or remoted.

docs.title: Userspace tunnel (the no-root default)
docs.text:
The default for RSD-required commands on iOS 17.4+ over USB. The kernel interface is replaced by a pure-Python TCP/IP stack (pmd-pytcp) running on the process's own event loop — no root anywhere, and no kernel TCP anywhere:

flowchart TB
    subgraph proc["pymobiledevice3 process"]
        svc["Developer services<br/>(DVT, os_trace, AFC, ...)"]
        rsd["RemoteServiceDiscoveryService<br/><i>open_connection = dial plane</i>"]
        dp["UserspaceDialPlane<br/>one socketpair relay per connection<br/>(no listener)"]
        stack["pmd-pytcp<br/>pure-asyncio TCP/IP stack"]
        tun["UserspaceTun<br/>L2 bridge: datagram socketpair<br/>+ 14-byte Ethernet shim"]
        cdp["CoreDeviceProxy transport<br/>(lockdown service connection)"]
    end
    usbmuxd["usbmuxd<br/>(unix socket)"]
    dev["iOS device<br/>RSD + services at fdxx::1"]

    svc --> rsd --> dp
    dp <-->|"pytcp TCP session<br/>over the tunnel"| stack
    stack <--> tun
    tun <-->|"encrypted tunnel frames"| cdp
    cdp <--> usbmuxd <-->|USB| dev

Key properties that fall out of this shape:

  • No root anywhere — there is no kernel interface; the "network" to the device lives entirely inside the process.
  • The tunnel address is in-process only. fdxx::1 exists on the pytcp stack, not in the kernel routing table, so external tools cannot reach it — the RSD reports this via is_in_process_tunnel.
  • One tunnel per process. The pytcp stack is a process-global singleton; every open/close transition serializes on a lifecycle lock, and concurrent establish_userspace_rsd() callers share the winning tunnel instead of racing it.

docs.title: Dialing a service connection
docs.text:
Services call the RSD's injected open_connection, which creates a socketpair(), hands one end to the caller and starts a relay task on the other:

sequenceDiagram
    participant S as ServiceConnection
    participant D as dial()
    participant H as relay task
    participant P as pytcp socket
    participant Dev as device service

    S->>D: open_connection(fdxx::1, port)
    D->>D: socketpair()
    D->>H: spawn relay task (port, other end)
    D-->>S: (reader, writer)
    H->>P: connect_tcp(fdxx::1, port)
    P->>Dev: SYN ... over the tunnel
    loop two pump tasks
        S->>P: bytes (client → device)
        P->>S: bytes (device → client)
    end
    Note over H,P: client EOF fully closes the pytcp socket<br/>(FIN reaches the device — orphan reaper owns the tail)<br/>device EOF reaches the client as write_eof

Why a socketpair for the hand-off: nothing listens, so no other process can reach the device's services through the relay (a loopback TCP listener was connectable by any local process for the tunnel's whole lifetime). It also never depends on how the platform completes a connect: iSH's AF_UNIX connect blocks until the peer accepts, which deadlocked the event loop when the dial plane accepted its own connections (#2068). On Windows CPython emulates socketpair() over loopback TCP and verifies the peer before returning it.

docs.title: Device disconnect and teardown
docs.text:
Nothing on the relay path can detect a vanished device (both relay endpoints are the same process, so keep-alive would only probe the local kernel), so the tunnel watches its own transport: when the CoreDeviceProxy connection dies — USB unplug makes usbmuxd close it immediately — a watcher task tears the whole tunnel down, surfacing errors to every blocked service read within about a second:

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as usbmuxd
    participant T as transport read task
    participant W as transport watcher
    participant A as aclose()
    participant DP as dial plane
    participant S as blocked service reads

    U--xT: connection closed (unplug)
    T->>W: wait_closed() returns
    W->>A: tear down (serialized on the lifecycle lock)
    A->>DP: __aexit__
    DP->>DP: cancel relay tasks, let pending FINs leave
    DP->>S: EOF / connection error
    Note over S: e.g. `dvt oslog` exits ~1 s after the cable is pulled

Teardown details worth knowing when reading the code:

  • The dial plane sets a _closing gate so no new relay starts, then cancels every in-flight relay task (a relay parked on device traffic never finishes on its own, issue #1756), repeating the cancel because Python <= 3.11 can swallow a cancellation that races an inner future. It then waits briefly for the FINs of just-closed connections to leave before the stack stops, so the device does not keep stale connections.
  • aclose() returning means the process-global stack is really stopped: an explicit close that races the watcher's teardown waits for it instead of returning early, so close-then-reopen is safe.
  • The CLI keeps its tunnel for the process lifetime and closes it at interpreter exit (~3 ms), so the device always sees clean FINs.

docs.title: Native remoted tunnel (macOS only)
docs.text:
--native (or PYMOBILEDEVICE3_NATIVE=1) reaches the RSD by piggybacking Apple's own remoted tunnel instead of building one. It needs no root, no entitlement and no Xcode, and does not suspend remoted (contrast the kernel/bonjour path; see the callout above).

It competes with remoted for the device

The device's remoted treats every incoming RSD connection from the same source IP (port ignored) as the same peer, and replaces that peer's existing connection with the new one before reading any handshake. On this tunnel remoted and pymobiledevice3 connect from the same host address, so opening ours evicts remoted's (Device connection interrupted in its log); remoted redials about a second later and evicts ours back. No handshake field changes this. On iOS 27.2+ the device also re-attaches (closing every advertised service port) when a peer's handshake UUID differs from the one it last sent, so ours has to present remoted's UUID here.

Commands therefore fail intermittently (ConnectionResetError, or ConnectionRefusedError after a re-attach), and after a few rounds remoted stops redialing, so Xcode/devicectl lose the device until remoted restarts or the device is replugged (#1994). This is why the native tunnel is opt-in: the userspace tunnel brings up a tunnel of its own, with its own host address, so the device keeps it apart from remoted.

flowchart LR
    subgraph host["host (no root)"]
        cli["pymobiledevice3"]
        rp["remotepairingd<br/>(RemotePairing.framework)"]
        rd["remoted"]
    end
    dev["iOS device<br/>RSD + services at fdxx::1"]

    cli -->|"XPC: browse / CreateAssertion"| rp
    cli -->|"socket table<br/>(find remoted's RSD port)"| rd
    rp -.->|"keeps the tunnel alive"| rd
    rd -->|"encrypted CoreDevice tunnel"| dev
    cli -->|"TCP6 to [fdxx::1]:rsd_port<br/>(kernel-routable)"| dev

How it works (all via ctypes + libxpc, no pyobjc):

  1. Ask com.apple.CoreDevice.remotepairingd (provided by the base-OS RemotePairing.framework, present on stock macOS — it backs iPhone Mirroring — not the Xcode-only CoreDevice.framework) to browse for the device and open its per-device XPC endpoint.
  2. RemotePairing.CreateAssertionCommand returns the device's in-tunnel tunnelIPAddress and an assertion identifier that keeps Apple's tunnel up for as long as the handle is held.
  3. Find the in-tunnel RSD port by matching remoted's own TCP connection to that tunnel address in the net.inet.tcp.pcblist_n socket table (no root). Starting with macOS 27, the kernel shows other processes' sockets only to a platform binary whose non-platform ancestors are all Apple or Developer ID signed, which hides root-owned remoted from us and from any sysctl we spawn directly. So /usr/sbin/sysctl is run double-forked: once launchd adopts it, it has no other ancestors and sees the whole table. If the table still comes back without a single connection, the scan falls back to one nettop -L 1 -m tcp sample, which sees every socket only because nettop is Apple-signed with com.apple.private.network.statistics (about 4x slower).

  4. Connect a normal TCP socket to [tunnelIPAddress]:rsd_port — the tunnel address is kernel-routable — and run the standard RSD handshake.

  5. Root: not required. Xcode: not required.

  6. Running as root anyway (CI runners, LaunchDaemons): remotepairingd is an XPCService declaring ServiceType = User, so launchd registers it per-uid, in a logged-in user's domain and never in the system/root domain. Whether a root process can reach it depends entirely on which bootstrap namespace it inherited, not on its uid: plain sudo from a logged-in user's terminal inherits that user's namespace and works unchanged, while a LaunchDaemon or anything under launchctl asuser 0 lands in a domain where the service is simply not registered and gets XPC_ERROR_CONNECTION_INVALID back.

So the ordinary lookup is always tried first, and only if the daemon reports the service missing is another uid's domain searched, via the libxpc SPI xpc_connection_set_target_uid. That keeps the process root — it reaches selectively into one domain rather than relocating itself — and it reacts to what actually happened instead of guessing from the uid. The probe is free: the error arrives about 0.2 ms after xpc_connection_activate, not at a timeout. The outcome is memoized per process, so later browses go straight to the domain that answered.

The retry resolves the uid from the console user (owner of /dev/console). On a host with no console user — a headless CI runner — set PYMOBILEDEVICE3_NATIVE_TARGET_UID to the uid that holds the pairing; that also seeds the memo, skipping the first attempt entirely. Setting it to 0 pins the ordinary lookup and disables retargeting. The SPI is root-only and traps the process when a non-root caller invokes it, so a seeded uid is refused with a warning unless the effective uid is 0. - Reachability: the tunnel address is a real kernel route (Apple's tunnel), so unlike the userspace tunnel it is reachable by other tools; it lives only while the handle (its assertion) is held. remote start-tunnel --native publishes this address for other processes (no sudo; without --native it builds the classic root tunnel). --rsd recognizes such an address by the interface it routes through (remotectl dumpstate names remoted's) and presents remoted's UUID there, like --native does. remote browse lists the devices remotepairingd reports — that is the macOS default, since browsing opens no RSD connection (--no-native forces the bonjour browse). - When it is used: only when asked for (--native, PYMOBILEDEVICE3_NATIVE=1, or PYMOBILEDEVICE3_DEFAULT_FALLBACK=native), and automatically for iOS 17.0-17.3 on macOS, which the userspace tunnel cannot serve (no CoreDeviceProxy). The built-in default everywhere is the userspace tunnel. - Changing the preference: PYMOBILEDEVICE3_DEFAULT_FALLBACK=native|userspace|tunneld sets which transport the automatic selection prefers. Set it to native to prefer this tunnel, or tunneld to route to the privileged daemon. - Throughput: rides the kernel-routable tunnel, so it avoids the userspace stack's per-packet Python overhead. Fair same-device AFC comparison on a physical iPhone 17-class device: device->host is USB-bound and on par with the userspace tunnel (~36 MB/s both), while host->device is ~1.8x faster (~36 vs ~20 MB/s — the userspace stack keeps its send segments deliberately small) and per-request latency is ~1.6x lower (~8 vs ~13 ms). All with no root.

docs.title: Device auxiliary metadata (RemoteServiceDiscoveryService.auxiliary_metadata)
docs.text:
Alongside the tunnel, the pairing layer carries the device's deviceKVSData — a binary-plist key-value store keyed by preference domain (e.g. com.apple.WebInspector, com.apple.mobile.wireless_lockdown), plus a NULL bucket of loose device properties. It is not part of the RSD handshake (peer_info); it rides the RemotePairing handshake / the host remotepairingd. When the transport that built the RSD had it, it is decoded onto RemoteServiceDiscoveryService.auxiliary_metadata ({domain: {key: value}}), with get_auxiliary_metadata(domain) and a typed is_remote_web_inspector_enabled() (whether Safari/WebKit remote inspection is enabled — no service is opened) reading from it.

Availability differs by transport, because only some perform a metadata-carrying pairing handshake:

  • Native (--native, macOS): the host remotepairingd exposes its merged, persisted KVS, which reliably includes com.apple.WebInspector. is_remote_web_inspector_enabled() returns a real True/False here.
  • tunneld / RemotePairing-over-bonjour: the RemotePairing handshake carries the device's base KVS. A fresh handshake omits lazily-registered domains like com.apple.WebInspector, so is_remote_web_inspector_enabled() is typically None (unknown).
  • Userspace (the no-root default, CoreDeviceProxy, iOS 17.4+): the tunnel is established without a pair-verify handshake, so no deviceKVSData is exchanged — auxiliary_metadata is empty and the helper returns None.

None means unknown on this transport, not disabled. Use --native on macOS when you need a definitive Web Inspector answer.

From the CLI, pymobiledevice3 remote auxiliary-metadata prints the whole decoded map as JSON (it uses the same transport selection as rsd-info, so pass --native on macOS for the full map):

pymobiledevice3 remote auxiliary-metadata --native | jq '.["com.apple.WebInspector"].EnableRemoteInspection'

docs.title: Capturing Network Traffic (pcap)
docs.text:
pymobiledevice3 pcap records every packet an iPhone or iPad sends and receives, on every interface (Wi-Fi, cellular, VPN, loopback), and labels each packet with the process that sent or received it. It needs no jailbreak, no Developer Mode, no Xcode and no Mac, and runs the same on macOS, Linux and Windows. It uses the device's built-in pcapd service, the same one behind Apple's macOS-only rvictl.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
Connect the device over USB, unlock it and trust the computer, then:

pymobiledevice3 pcap --out capture.pcapng

Use the device, press Ctrl+C to stop, and open capture.pcapng in Wireshark. While capturing, each packet is also printed to the terminal (a one-line summary plus a hex dump); without --out, that terminal output is all you get.

The file is always pcapng

The output is written in the pcapng format whatever extension you give it, because pcapng is what carries the per-packet process labels. Name it .pcapng so every tool recognizes it.

docs.title: Filtering while you capture
docs.text:
Option Keeps only packets... Example --process NAME_OR_PID owned by this process (exact name, or PID) --process MobileSafari -i, --interface NAME on this interface (en0), or on all units of one (en) -i en0 -c, --count N ...and stops after N of them -c 200

The options combine:

# The first 200 Wi-Fi packets of Safari
pymobiledevice3 pcap --process MobileSafari -i en0 -c 200 --out safari.pcapng
  • Process names are the executable names the kernel reports (as pymobiledevice3 processes ps shows them), not the app's display name, and are truncated to 16 characters. Matching is exact and case-sensitive. A PID only matches while that process runs, so the name is usually the better choice.
  • Interfaces you will typically see: en0 (Wi-Fi), pdp_ip0 and friends (cellular), utun0... (VPNs and system tunnels), lo0 (loopback). Capture without -i first to see which ones carry traffic on your device.

docs.title: Which process sent this packet?
docs.text:
Every packet in the file carries a comment like:

PID: 312, ProcName: nsurlsessiond, EPID: 1045, EProcName: MyApp, SVC: 0
  • ProcName / PID is the process that owns the socket.
  • EProcName / EPID is the effective process: the one the traffic is really for. iOS often lets a system daemon do networking on an app's behalf (for example nsurlsessiond for background transfers). Then ProcName is the daemon and EProcName is the app. For ordinary traffic both name the same process.

--process matches ProcName only. To find everything an app caused, including work delegated to daemons, capture without --process and filter on EProcName afterwards.

docs.title: In Wireshark
docs.text:
Wireshark shows the comment under Packet comments in the packet details. Right-click it and choose Apply as Column to see the process next to every packet. Display filters:

frame.comment contains "EProcName: MyApp,"
frame.comment matches "^PID: [0-9]+, ProcName: MobileSafari,"

The first keeps everything done for MyApp; the second keeps only packets whose socket MobileSafari itself owns. The trailing comma stops MyApp from also matching MyAppExtension.

docs.title: With tshark
docs.text:
tshark (Wireshark's command-line tool) can answer the common questions directly:

# Packets per effective process, busiest first
tshark -r capture.pcapng -T fields -e frame.comment \
  | sed -E 's/.*EProcName: ([^,]*),.*/\1/' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

# Which hosts did each process connect to over TLS (from the SNI)
tshark -r capture.pcapng -Y tls.handshake.extensions_server_name \
  -T fields -e frame.comment -e tls.handshake.extensions_server_name

# DNS lookups and who asked for them
tshark -r capture.pcapng -Y "dns.flags.response == 0" -T fields -e frame.comment -e dns.qry.name

docs.title: Live capture in Wireshark
docs.text:
On macOS and Linux, point Wireshark at a named pipe and let pymobiledevice3 write into it:

mkfifo /tmp/ios.pcapng
wireshark -k -i /tmp/ios.pcapng &
pymobiledevice3 pcap --out /tmp/ios.pcapng > /dev/null

Packets appear in Wireshark as they arrive (> /dev/null silences the terminal copy). On macOS, wireshark is /Applications/Wireshark.app/Contents/MacOS/Wireshark unless you installed the command-line wrapper.

docs.title: What a capture shows
docs.text:
• Encrypted traffic (HTTPS, QUIC, most app traffic) shows its endpoints, sizes, timing and the TLS server name, not its contents. DNS queries are usually readable.
  • Packets from interfaces without an Ethernet header (cellular, VPN, loopback) get a placeholder Ethernet header with the address be:ef:be:ef:be:ef so every pcap tool can open the file. That address is not real hardware.
  • The capture includes everything on the device, possibly personal data. Treat capture files as sensitive.

docs.title: From Python
docs.text:
import asyncio

from pymobiledevice3.lockdown import create_using_usbmux
from pymobiledevice3.services.pcapd import PcapdService


async def main():
    async with await create_using_usbmux() as lockdown, PcapdService(lockdown) as pcap:
        async for packet in pcap.watch(packets_count=20):
            print(packet.comm, packet.ecomm, packet.interface_name, len(packet.data))

        # Or write a pcapng file, with the same filters as the CLI
        with open("capture.pcapng", "wb") as out:
            await pcap.write_to_pcap(out, pcap.watch(packets_count=100, process="MobileSafari"))


asyncio.run(main())

See the PcapdService reference for every field of a captured packet.

docs.title: Python API
docs.text:
Besides the CLI, pymobiledevice3 is a library. Everything the CLI does is built on the same public classes you can use directly from your own code.

Install it into your project's environment (pip install pymobiledevice3 or uv add pymobiledevice3), connect the device over USB, and accept the Trust This Computer prompt the first time you connect. See Installation for platform notes.

The API is asyncio-based

Connection helpers and service methods are coroutines. Run them inside an event loop, e.g. with asyncio.run(main()).

docs.title: 1. Connect to a device
docs.text:
Every service is created on top of a service provider, the object that knows how to reach the device. There are two kinds: a lockdown connection (LockdownClient, over usbmux), and an RSD connection (RemoteServiceDiscoveryService, RemoteServiceDiscovery over an iOS 17+ tunnel). Pick based on the iOS version and the service you need:

Connection Python entry point iOS Root? Use when Lockdown (USB / Wi-Fi) create_using_usbmux all no Classic services: AFC, app install, syslog, diagnostics, backup, profiles RSD, best no-root tunnel PreferredRsdTunnel 17+ no Default for developer/DVT: the userspace tunnel, falling back to the native tunnel for iOS 17.0-17.3 on macOS RSD, native (macOS) NativeRemotedTunnel 17+ no macOS only: piggybacks Apple's remoted; faster host->device, but evicts and is evicted by remoted's own connection (#1994) RSD, userspace UserspaceRsdTunnel 17+ no Cross-platform in-process tunnel; the tunnel address is reachable only from this process RSD, tunneld get_tunneld_devices 17+ yes (daemon) You need a shared/persistent tunnel, or an external tool (e.g. lldb) must reach the device

Rule of thumb: need a developer/DVT service on iOS 17+? Use PreferredRsdTunnel, which picks the best no-root transport for the host. Everything else goes over lockdown. Classic lockdown services work over USB on every iOS version (developer services did too, until iOS 17 moved them behind RSD). The sections below show each path.

docs.title: Over USB (lockdown)
docs.text:
import asyncio

from pymobiledevice3.lockdown import create_using_usbmux


async def main():
    async with await create_using_usbmux() as lockdown:
        print(lockdown.all_values)  # full device info dict


asyncio.run(main())

create_using_usbmux(serial=...) targets a specific device by UDID; omit it to pick the first one.

docs.title: iOS 17+ developer services (tunnel)
docs.text:
Developer/DVT services on iOS 17+ require an RSD tunnel.

Preferred: PreferredRsdTunnel. It uses the in-process userspace tunnel and, on macOS, falls back automatically to the native tunnel (piggybacking Apple's remoted) for iOS 17.0-17.3, which the userspace tunnel cannot serve. No sudo and no separate tunneld daemon. It is an async context manager that yields a connected RemoteServiceDiscoveryService:

import asyncio

from pymobiledevice3.remote.rsd_tunnel import PreferredRsdTunnel


async def main():
    # serial=None -> first device; prefer_native=True tries the macOS native tunnel first
    async with PreferredRsdTunnel(serial=None) as rsd:
        print(rsd.udid, rsd.product_version)
        # `rsd` now drives any developer service / DvtProvider


asyncio.run(main())

To choose the transport explicitly, use UserspaceRsdTunnel (from pymobiledevice3.remote.userspace_tunnel, cross-platform) or NativeRemotedTunnel (from pymobiledevice3.remote.native_tunnel, macOS only). All three tunnel classes take serial= and work either as async context managers or through explicit aopen() / aclose() calls. Caveats:

  • One userspace tunnel per process, and its device address is reachable only from this process, so don't hand it to external tools such as lldb.
  • The native tunnel's address is kernel-routable, so it has no such limitation. But on that tunnel the device keeps a single RSD connection, which ours and remoted's keep evicting from each other; this can leave Xcode/devicectl without the device.

The CLI's --userspace flag goes through establish_userspace_rsd(), which opens a userspace tunnel and keeps it alive until the process exits. It suits short scripts that never tear the tunnel down; embedders should prefer UserspaceRsdTunnel for explicit teardown:

from pymobiledevice3.remote.userspace_tunnel import establish_userspace_rsd


async def main():
    rsd = await establish_userspace_rsd()  # connected RemoteServiceDiscoveryService
    print(rsd.product_version)

Alternative: reuse a running tunneld. If a privileged tunneld is already running, discover its published tunnels instead:

import asyncio

from pymobiledevice3.tunneld.api import get_tunneld_devices


async def main():
    rsds = await get_tunneld_devices()
    try:
        rsd = rsds[0]
        print(rsd.udid, rsd.product_version)
    finally:
        for rsd in rsds:
            await rsd.close()


asyncio.run(main())

You can also wrap an explicit address with RemoteServiceDiscoveryService((host, port)) and use it as an async context manager. See iOS 17+ tunnels for how the tunnel is established.

docs.title: 2. The service pattern
docs.text:
Nearly every service subclasses LockdownService, takes a service provider, and is an async context manager: entering it opens the service connection and leaving it closes it. A few, like CrashReportsManager and DvtProvider, wrap other services instead. Once you know this pattern, the services all work the same way:

import asyncio

from pymobiledevice3.lockdown import create_using_usbmux
from pymobiledevice3.services.os_trace import OsTraceService


async def main():
    async with await create_using_usbmux() as lockdown, OsTraceService(lockdown) as os_trace:
        async for entry in os_trace.syslog():
            print(entry.pid, entry.image_name, entry.message)


asyncio.run(main())

The same service classes accept an RSD as well, so OsTraceService(rsd) works over a tunnel too.

docs.title: 3. Worked examples
docs.text: These snippets go inside an async def like main() above, with lockdown an open service provider.

docs.title: Stream syslog
docs.text:
from pymobiledevice3.services.os_trace import OsTraceService

async with OsTraceService(lockdown) as os_trace:
    async for entry in os_trace.syslog():
        print(f"[{entry.level.name}] {entry.image_name}: {entry.message}")

docs.title: List installed apps
docs.text:
from pymobiledevice3.services.installation_proxy import InstallationProxyService

async with InstallationProxyService(lockdown) as installation_proxy:
    apps = await installation_proxy.get_apps()
for bundle_id, info in apps.items():
    print(bundle_id, info.get("CFBundleShortVersionString"))

docs.title: Browse files over AFC
docs.text:
AFC (Apple File Conduit) gives access to the device's media directory:

from pymobiledevice3.services.afc import AfcService

async with AfcService(lockdown) as afc:
    print(await afc.listdir("/"))

docs.title: Run a DVT (developer) service
docs.text:
DVT services go through a DvtProvider. On iOS 17+ it needs an RSD from a tunnel. It also needs Developer Mode enabled (iOS 16+), and on iOS < 17 the Developer Disk Image mounted (pymobiledevice3 mounter auto-mount). Each instrument is itself an async context manager:

from pymobiledevice3.services.dvt.instruments.dvt_provider import DvtProvider
from pymobiledevice3.services.dvt.instruments.process_control import ProcessControl

# `rsd` is a tunnel-backed service provider (see "Connect to a device" above)
async with DvtProvider(rsd) as dvt, ProcessControl(dvt) as process_control:
    pid = await process_control.launch("com.apple.mobilesafari")
    print("launched pid", pid)

docs.title: 4. Finding the right service
docs.text:
There are dozens of services under pymobiledevice3/services/. A few common ones:

Task Class Module Syslog / oslog / process list OsTraceService services.os_trace App install / list / uninstall InstallationProxyService services.installation_proxy File access (media / app containers) AfcService services.afc Diagnostics, reboot, IORegistry DiagnosticsService services.diagnostics SpringBoard icons / wallpaper / orientation SpringBoardServicesService services.springboard Crash reports CrashReportsManager services.crash_reports Mount the Developer Disk Image MobileImageMounterService services.mobile_image_mounter DVT instruments (iOS 17+ via tunnel) DvtProvider services.dvt.instruments.dvt_provider

For the full surface, see the API reference. The Writing CLI commands guide shows how the CLI wires service providers into commands.

docs.title: 5. Faster imports on Python 3.15+
docs.text:
On Python 3.15+ the CLI enables PEP 810 lazy imports for itself, scoped so that only pymobiledevice3's own imports are deferred, which roughly halves its startup time. As a library, pymobiledevice3 never changes your process's import semantics: importing pymobiledevice3.* from your application stays eager.

If you own the process, you can opt in to the same behavior. It saves ~0.2-0.3s on the heaviest entry points (e.g. pymobiledevice3.remote.userspace_tunnel), and the filter keeps every other package eager, since process-wide laziness is known to break some import hooks:

import sys


def _lazy_filter(importing: str, imported: str, fromlist: object = None) -> bool:
    return importing.partition(".")[0] == "pymobiledevice3"


if hasattr(sys, "set_lazy_imports"):  # Python 3.15+
    sys.set_lazy_imports("all")
    sys.set_lazy_imports_filter(_lazy_filter)

Run this before importing any pymobiledevice3 module. On older Pythons it is a no-op.

docs.title: Restoring and updating devices
docs.text:
pymobiledevice3 restore update reimplements the host side of an IPSW restore (an IPSW is Apple's firmware package for a device): what Finder, iTunes, Xcode and idevicerestore do when they flash a device. This guide explains the choices the command offers, what happens on the device, and which requests go to Apple's signing server (TSS) along the way. The measured numbers come from an iPhone18,4 on iOS 27.0 (build 24A435); they differ per device.

Restoring can erase your device

restore update --erase is a factory reset: everything on the device is deleted. Even a plain update in place reflashes the whole firmware, and an interrupted or failed restore can leave the device in recovery mode, where getting it back may take an erase. Make a backup first (pymobiledevice3 backup2 backup <directory>) and keep the cable connected until the device has rebooted. After an erase the device goes through setup again, including Activation Lock if Find My was on.

Before you start you need:

  • The device connected over USB (restore does not work over Wi-Fi).
  • Network access to Apple's signing server (gs.apple.com), and to ipsw.me or AppleDB when you let the tool pick the firmware.
  • A build Apple still signs for the device (see Choosing the firmware).
  • Several GB of free disk space for the IPSW.
  • On Linux and Windows, libusb for recovery and DFU mode (see Installation).

Two device modes come up throughout: recovery mode is the iBoot bootloader waiting for firmware from a computer; DFU mode (Device Firmware Update) is a lower-level mode run by the chip's boot ROM, used when even iBoot cannot start.

The simplest run updates the connected device in place to a signed build you pick from a list:

pymobiledevice3 restore update

docs.title: What a restore does
docs.text:
1. Normal mode. The device is found through usbmuxd. Its build, ECID (the chip's unique ID), AP and SEP nonces and the peripheral state (PreflightInfo) are read over lockdown, and the AP ticket is requested from TSS. Only then is the device sent into recovery mode.
  2. Recovery. iBSS/iBEC are uploaded and the device is booted into the restore ramdisk from the IPSW.
  3. Restore mode. The ramdisk's restored asks the host for everything it needs, item by item: the root filesystem, firmware components, per-peripheral tickets, the baseband, cryptexes. The host answers each request, proxying FDR (Factory Data Recovery, the device's factory calibration data) traffic in between. This phase is where all the time goes.
  4. Reboot into the new build.

If the device is already in recovery or DFU mode, step 1 is skipped: the tool waits for such a device, identifies it by ECID (--ecid picks one when several are connected) and starts from step 2. Nothing that needs lockdown is available then, so anything derived from PreflightInfo (including --tss-batch, below) is simply not done.

docs.title: Choosing the firmware
docs.text:
-i / --ipsw accepts a local path or an http(s):// URL. A URL is downloaded to a temporary directory and deleted after the restore. With -i omitted, the tool asks ipsw.me for the builds Apple currently signs for the device's product type and lets you pick one interactively; that needs network access and works from normal mode as well as recovery (the product type comes from lockdown or from the recovery-mode device table).

To stop downloading the same multi-GB IPSW on every run, pass --ipsw-dir (or set PYMOBILEDEVICE3_IPSW_DIR once; a leading ~ is expanded). Downloads then go into that directory under Apple's filename (e.g. iPhone12,1_27.2_24B119_Restore.ipsw) and are kept. A file already there with that name is used as-is, without re-hashing, and the interactive picker marks such builds (local). A new download is written to <name>.part, which a later run resumes after an interruption, and is renamed into place only once it matches its SHA-256 (the one Apple's CDN publishes for the file, else ipsw.me's); a mismatching download is discarded. A single Ctrl-C stops the download and keeps the .part. If ipsw.me can't be reached, the picker reports it and exits.

--beta lists the newest beta builds instead, from AppleDB (ipsw.me has no betas), restricted to those with an IPSW for the device: e.g. 27.2 beta 4: 24B5110a. AppleDB's signing status is shown as (unsigned) but is only a hint; TSS decides at restore time. --ipsw-dir, resuming and SHA-256 verification work the same way.

Whatever the source, the build must be signed by Apple at restore time, since the AP ticket comes from TSS. A --tss SHSH blob can be supplied for the AP ticket instead of asking TSS; the peripheral tickets are still requested live.

docs.title: Update or erase
docs.text:
By default the restore is an update in place: the Upgrade Install (IPSW) build identity is used, the data volume is kept, and the device comes back with its apps and settings. --erase selects the Erase Install (IPSW) identity instead: a factory reset that recreates the filesystem and deletes all data on the device. Both go through the same steps above; erase is what you want for a device stuck in recovery with no usable data volume, or to wipe it.

Some IPSWs have several identities matching that name for the same device, for example the cloudOS (Private Cloud Compute) research IPSW, where Darwin Cloud Customer Erase Install (IPSW) comes before Research Darwin Cloud Customer Erase Install (IPSW). --variant picks an identity by its exact name instead (restore tss accepts it too):

pymobiledevice3 restore update --erase --ipsw <ipsw> \
    --variant "Research Darwin Cloud Customer Erase Install (IPSW)"

--ignore-fdr is a debugging option: the host connects to the FDR service but does not proxy its traffic.

docs.title: Restoring from DFU mode
docs.text:
DFU mode is entered with a button sequence; the host cannot enter it alone. --dfu walks you through it before the restore starts, and restore enter-dfu does just that part:

pymobiledevice3 restore update -i iPhone.ipsw --dfu
pymobiledevice3 restore enter-dfu

The guide picks the buttons for the model (iPhones by product type; for an iPad it asks whether there is a Home button), counts each step down, and watches the device over USB: its screen going black, then the device coming back in DFU mode (classic DFU, or Debug USB/KIS on A16 and later), in recovery, or booted normally. Each step moves on as soon as the device reacts, and if it ends up anywhere but DFU the guide says what to change and offers another try. Apple documents only the recovery mode sequences; the DFU ones are the widely used sequences.

On an iPhone 8 or later that is booted, the host restarts the phone itself, so the quick VOLUME UP, VOLUME DOWN, SIDE presses go away: you hold VOLUME DOWN, the phone restarts, you add SIDE once it went down, then release SIDE. --manual keeps the full button sequence instead.

On macOS, an A16-or-later device in DFU mode (Debug USB/KIS) can only be opened by Apple's deviceinterfaced, so the restore loads its images through that daemon; elsewhere it talks KIS to the device over libusb.

docs.title: Keeping deviceinterfaced off the device
docs.text: macOS's deviceinterfaced can claim the USB device while it re-enumerates during a restore, so the device in DFU mode is never seen. --exclusive-usb (experimental, macOS only) keeps the daemon off for the restore: it boots it out, or keeps killing it where System Integrity Protection refuses that, and loads and starts it again when the restore ends. The launchctl calls run through sudo and may prompt for your password. It cannot be used with an A16-or-later device in DFU mode on macOS, which is reached through that daemon.

docs.title: How the host reaches the device
docs.text:
On macOS, devices in recovery and DFU mode are reached through IOKit; elsewhere through libusb. A16-or-later devices in DFU mode go through deviceinterfaced on macOS (see above). restore --libusb (or PYMOBILEDEVICE3_USB_BACKEND=libusb) switches macOS to libusb, e.g. to compare the two:

pymobiledevice3 restore --libusb update -i iPhone.ipsw

docs.title: Several devices at once
docs.text:
Each restore stays on its own device, so several can run side by side: start one restore update per device. With more than one device connected, the command asks which one to use; --ecid picks it non-interactively. On devices from the A12 on, the UDID is <ChipID>-<ECID>, so the ECID is the part after the dash:

# UDID 00008150-001074523440401C
pymobiledevice3 restore update --ecid 0x001074523440401C -i iPhone18,4_Restore.ipsw

lockdown info reports it as UniqueChipID (decimal), and the --ecid option takes either form.

docs.title: The helper commands
docs.text:
• restore enter puts a normal-mode device into recovery, where it stays until restore exit re-enables auto-boot and reboots it back to iOS; restore restart reboots either (see below for --vdm).
  • restore tss requests (and with --out saves) the AP ticket for a build without restoring, --behavior Update|Erase or --variant selecting the identity.
  • restore ramdisk boots the IPSW's restore ramdisk and stops there.
  • restore shell opens an IPython shell with the iBoot (irecv) client of a recovery/DFU device.

docs.title: Restarting over USB-C (macOS)
docs.text:
restore restart --vdm restarts the device with Apple's USB Power Delivery reboot message, sent by the Mac's own USB-C port controller. The device's USB-C controller handles it, not iOS, so it needs no pairing or trust and works in recovery mode too:

sudo pymobiledevice3 restore restart --vdm
  • It needs root: only root can open the port controller.
  • The device has to be on a Thunderbolt/USB4 port, the ports with Apple's PD controller, and connected directly: a hub in between does not pass the message on.
  • With several Apple devices on such ports, the command asks which one to restart; --ecid picks it non-interactively.

docs.title: Inspecting the preflight data
docs.text:
Two commands expose what the device reports before a restore, in JSON:

# what lockdown reports in normal mode: PreflightInfo (each peripheral updater's
# identity fields and current nonce), FirmwarePreflightInfo, ApParameters
pymobiledevice3 restore preflight

# the TSS request each updater would send, built by the device itself for this
# IPSW (restoreserviced over a tunnel; uploads each updater's firmware first)
pymobiledevice3 restore preflight-requests -i iPhone.ipsw --updater T200 --updater Rose

preflight-requests returns, per updater, the request (DeviceInfoRequests), its ticket and manifest tags (DeviceInfoTags) and the updaters whose preflight failed (DeviceInfoFailures; the baseband always does in normal mode). Without --updater it queries every known updater except the baseband. It is what --tss-batch is validated against: a chip can only be served from the prefetch if the request pymobiledevice3 builds from PreflightInfo equals the one the device builds, nonce aside.

docs.title: TSS requests during a restore
docs.text:
Every restore signs firmware against gs.apple.com. Without any flag:

  1. The AP request, in normal mode, before the device enters recovery. It asks for ApImg4Ticket against the ECID, the AP and SEP nonces and the build manifest. When the build identity has a RecoveryVariant, a second AP request follows for the recoveryOS root ticket.
  2. One request per peripheral updater, during the restore. restored asks for each chip's ticket with a FirmwareUpdaterData message; on iOS 18 and later the device builds the TSS request itself (DeviceGeneratedRequest) and the host adds the manifest digests and forwards it. On this device that is T200 (battery management), Rose (UWB), Centauri (Wi-Fi/Bluetooth), Savage (Face ID, two loops), SE (Secure Element), Vinyl (eSIM), Baseband, and after FDR sealing Rose again plus Cryptex1 and its local policy: 11 requests.

That is 13 sequential requests of about half a second each for a full update on this device. Nothing is reused between restores: every chip carries a nonce and most regenerate it at every boot.

docs.title: The empty preflight message
docs.text: Before it asks for a chip's ticket, restored sends FirmwareUpdaterPreflight for that chip. It does so because the host's restore options declare PersonalizedDuringPreflight, which tells the device the host may already hold tickets from a personalization done in normal mode. Apple's own host only fills that stash for Apple displays (their USB-C and timing controllers); for iPhones it answers with an empty dictionary, and so does pymobiledevice3. The message is logged at debug level and is not a problem.

docs.title: --tss-batch
docs.text:
With the flag, the peripheral ticket requests are built up front from the device's lockdown PreflightInfo (each chip's identity fields and current nonce) plus the build manifest, and are sent inside the AP request. TSS answers every ticket in that one response, so the prefetch adds no request.

During the restore, when restored asks for a chip's ticket, the host compares the device's own request with what it signed, entry for entry (nonces, digests and flags included). Only an identical request is answered from the prefetch; any difference, or a request on which the device asks for a fresh personalization (MessageForceRepersonalization, or any loop but the first), goes to TSS as usual. A prefetched ticket is never served against a nonce the chip has since discarded.

At the end of the restore a summary is logged:

TSS PREFETCH SUMMARY
  prefetched up-front : 7 ['SE', 'Rose', 'Centauri', 'Savage', 'T200', 'Vinyl', 'Baseband']
  hits                : 3 ['T200', 'SE', 'Vinyl']
  request mismatches  : 5 ['Rose', 'Centauri', 'Baseband', 'Savage', 'Rose']
  not prefetched      : 0 []
  >> TSS requests saved during the restore: 3

A hit saves one request. A mismatch costs nothing: the request the reactive path would have made is made, and the log line names the entries that differed (on this device always the chip's nonce). Which chips hit depends on whether the chip keeps its nonce across the boot into the restore ramdisk:

Chip Nonce across the boot into the ramdisk Outcome T200, SE, Vinyl kept served from the prefetch Rose, Centauri, Baseband, Savage regenerated live request, as without the flag Cryptex1 not exposed before the restore never prefetched

Request count per restore on this device: 13 without the flag, 10 with it.

If TSS ever rejects the AP request because of a prefetched entry, the AP request is retried alone and the restore proceeds with every chip on the live path. That is the only case in which the flag costs a request, and it happens before the device leaves normal mode. A chip whose request cannot be built is left to the live path.

The flag is opt-in because it relies on pymobiledevice3 reproducing each chip's request format from PreflightInfo; a format change in a future iOS build turns into misses, not into wrong tickets, and the miss log shows which entries no longer match. The per-chip request builders live in pymobiledevice3/restore/tss.py (PREFETCHABLE_UPDATERS); the tss-batch-prefetch skill in the repository describes how to validate and extend them.

docs.title: Mirroring and Controlling the Screen
docs.text:
pymobiledevice3 can show a device's screen live and let you use it from your computer: tap, swipe, type, press the hardware buttons, hear its audio and share the clipboard. There are two viewers:

  • serve-web: the screen in any modern browser, on macOS, Linux or Windows, with nothing else to install.
  • serve-vnc: a VNC server for macOS Screen Sharing or any VNC client (macOS hosts only).

Both use the same live video stream Xcode's device window uses, sent by the device itself over the iOS 17+ tunnel that pymobiledevice3 sets up for you.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• iOS 27 or later. Older versions don't send the stream, so both commands refuse to start.
  • Developer Mode turned on and the DeveloperDiskImage mounted (pymobiledevice3 mounter auto-mount; see Developer Mode and DDI).
  • No foreground app using the camera or microphone (see below).

docs.title: In the browser: serve-web
docs.text:
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device display serve-web

Open http://127.0.0.1:8080/. The device appears inside a phone frame, live:

  • Touch: click to tap, drag to swipe.
  • Hardware buttons are drawn on the edges of the frame; click them. The bar under the device adds Home, Siri and left/right swipes.
  • Keyboard: type into the page and the text goes to the device.
  • Sound plays in the browser (--no-audio starts muted; Enable Sound turns it back on).
  • View panel: zoom (Ctrl+= / Ctrl+- / Ctrl+0) and rotate the displayed device.
  • Screenshot (Ctrl+P) saves the current frame as a PNG.
  • Shortcuts & help (?) lists every keyboard shortcut.
  • Style and the Accessibility panel switch light/dark mode, text size, color filters, reduce motion, increase contrast and similar settings, like Xcode's environment overrides. They change the device's real settings and stay changed after you close the viewer; Reset all puts the accessibility settings back to their defaults.
  • Clipboard panel: turn on Sync, and text and images copied on the device land in your computer's clipboard, while whatever you copied on the computer is on the device by the time you paste. Pictures copied out of a rich-text app such as Notes are not shared (copy them from Photos instead). The browser only allows clipboard access on localhost or with --https, asks for permission once, and holds device copies made while the tab is in the background until you return.

Video is decoded in the browser itself (WebCodecs), which is why nothing needs to be installed on the viewing machine.

docs.title: Sharing with other machines
docs.text:
By default the viewer only listens on this computer. To reach it from the rest of the network, bind every interface and set a password, because whoever reaches the port can both watch and control the device:

pymobiledevice3 developer core-device display serve-web --bind 0.0.0.0 --password 'CHOOSE_ONE' --https

--https is needed when viewing from another machine: browsers only allow the in-browser video decoder on localhost or over HTTPS. The certificate is self-signed, so the browser warns once; accept it and the viewer works normally.

docs.title: With a VNC client: serve-vnc (macOS)
docs.text:
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device display serve-vnc

Then connect to vnc://127.0.0.1:5901, for example from Finder with ⌘K, which opens macOS Screen Sharing. This viewer is macOS-only because it decodes the video on the host with VideoToolbox.

In the VNC client On the device Click / drag Tap / swipe Right-click Home Ctrl+H / Ctrl+L Home / Lock Ctrl+[ / Ctrl+] Volume down / up Ctrl+\ Mute Ctrl+S Siri

Useful options:

  • --audio plays the device's sound through the Mac's speakers.
  • --share-clipboard shares text (VNC has no image clipboard). It follows the VNC client's own clipboard setting; clients with the Extended Clipboard extension (TigerVNC, noVNC, ...) get full UTF-8.
  • --bind 0.0.0.0 --password 'CHOOSE_ONE' makes it reachable from other machines, with the same warning as above.

docs.title: Devices with several displays
docs.text:
On a device with more than one built-in display, such as a foldable iPhone, both viewers show the display in use, and touches go to that display. Both follow the device as it is folded or unfolded, switching to the other display by themselves, and show an unfolded device in landscape when it is held that way. serve-vnc resizes the VNC client's screen for that, which needs a client supporting the DesktopSize extension (TigerVNC, noVNC, ...); other clients are disconnected and have to reconnect.

To show one display regardless, pass its displayId from get-display-info:

pymobiledevice3 developer core-device get-display-info
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device display serve-web --display-id 2

monitor-display-info prints the display information again each time it changes. The touch commands of universal-hid-service (tap, drag, ...) also act on the display in use; --touch-service-id picks another display's touchscreen, as listed by universal-hid-service list-connected.

docs.title: Camera and microphone
docs.text: iOS won't start a mirroring session while a foreground app is using the camera or microphone; Xcode has the same restriction. If Camera, Voice Memos or a similar app is in front, the command explains this in one line and exits. Quit that app and run it again. While mirroring is running, those apps can't use the sensors and record silence or black video, so stop mirroring before recording with them.

docs.title: Raw stream capture
docs.text:
For analysis or archiving, the stream can be saved as it arrives:

# Capture 10 seconds of the raw RTP/HEVC packets
pymobiledevice3 developer core-device display start-video-stream /tmp/cap.rtp --duration 10

# In a source checkout: convert to an .h265 file that ffplay or VLC can play
misc/rtp_dump.py /tmp/cap.rtp /tmp/cap.h265
ffplay -framerate 60 /tmp/cap.h265

start-audio-stream does the same for the device's sound.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Common failures mapped to their causes and fixes. Each section quotes the error message (or exception name) the CLI prints, so you can search this page for what you're seeing.

Start with doctor. It checks the host — whether usbmux is reachable and finds devices over Wi-Fi, whether mDNS queries can leave the machine, and which tunnel transports are usable — and, when a device is attached, what that device is: its model and OS version, whether it is paired, and whether developer mode and a developer disk image are in place. It needs no device, which is the point when nothing shows up at all, and it separates "this machine cannot discover devices" from "the device is not there":

pymobiledevice3 doctor

It exits non-zero when something is broken, and --json produces the same report as data. It never pairs, so running it cannot pop a trust dialog.

Please paste its output when opening an issue — it answers most of what would otherwise be asked in follow-up questions.

For any problem, running with increased verbosity usually reveals what is going on:

pymobiledevice3 -vv <command...>

docs.title: "Device is not connected" (NoDeviceConnectedError)
docs.text:
No device was found over usbmux (the host service, usbmuxd, that connects to iOS devices over USB and Wi-Fi).

  • Check the cable, unlock the device, and check that it shows up in pymobiledevice3 usbmux list.
  • On Linux, make sure usbmuxd is installed and running.
  • On Windows, install iTunes — it provides the Apple Mobile Device Service that pymobiledevice3 relies on. Prefer the classic installer over the Microsoft Store "Apple Devices" app: the Store app's service does not discover devices over Wi-Fi, so a device with no cable never appears in usbmux list.
  • If you passed --udid, verify it matches a connected device (see the next section).

docs.title: "Failed to connect to usbmuxd socket" (ConnectionFailedToUsbmuxdError)
docs.text:
The usbmuxd daemon itself is not reachable.

  • On Linux, start it: sudo systemctl start usbmuxd (or run usbmuxd -f in the foreground to see its logs).
  • On Windows, make sure the Apple Mobile Device Service is running.
  • If your daemon listens on a non-default address, point pymobiledevice3 at it with --usbmux HOST:PORT (or a unix socket path), or the PYMOBILEDEVICE3_USBMUX / USBMUXD_SOCKET_ADDRESS environment variables.

docs.title: "Device not found: ..." (DeviceNotFoundError)
docs.text:
The UDID you passed (via --udid or PYMOBILEDEVICE3_UDID) doesn't match any device known to the transport that was asked for it — the message names that transport (usbmux, tunneld, remotepairingd for the native tunnel). List what's actually connected:

pymobiledevice3 usbmux list

docs.title: The device is advertising over Wi-Fi but usbmux list does not show it
docs.text:
Two different things have to be true, and only the first lives on the device:

pymobiledevice3 bonjour mobdev2   # is the device announcing itself?
pymobiledevice3 usbmux list       # has this host's daemon listed it?

When the browse finds it and the listing does not, nothing is wrong on the device — the host's daemon has not picked the announcement up. EnableWifiConnections takes effect immediately when set, so re-running lockdown wifi-connections on will not change anything.

Three things to try, cheapest first:

  • Unplug and replug the cable, or toggle Wi-Fi off and on on the device. Both make the daemon re-discover, and it often recovers on its own given a minute.

  • Make the device re-announce itself, which costs nothing and does not change any setting:

    pymobiledevice3 notification post com.apple.mobile.lockdown.BonjourServiceChanged

    lockdownd (the device's pairing and service daemon) observes that notification, tears down its wireless connections and re-registers the Bonjour service. It is what lockdownd posts to itself after pair records change.

  • Confirm this host is paired with the device over USB. Wi-Fi reach is per host: the device advertises one authentication tag per paired host, so a machine that has never been cabled to it cannot recognise it however the setting is set.

If the browse finds nothing either, the setting really is off (or this host cannot send mDNS at all — see pymobiledevice3 doctor).

docs.title: "Waiting for the user to answer the Trust dialog on the device" (PairingDialogResponsePendingError)
docs.text: The device is showing the Trust This Computer? dialog. Unlock the device, tap Trust, enter the passcode if asked, and run the command again.

docs.title: "The user refused to trust this computer" (UserDeniedPairingError)
docs.text: Don't Trust was tapped. To make the dialog reappear, reset the device's trust decisions: Settings → General → Transfer or Reset iPhone → Reset → Reset Location & Privacy, then reconnect the cable.

docs.title: "The device is protected with a passcode. Unlock it and try again." (PasswordRequiredError)
docs.text: Pairing (and some lockdown operations) require the device to be unlocked. Unlock it and retry.

docs.title: "Device is not paired" (NotPairedError)
docs.text:
The host has no valid pair record for this device. Create one:

pymobiledevice3 lockdown pair

If pairing keeps failing with "The device does not recognize this computer's pairing record" (InvalidHostIDError), the device holds a stale record for this host — unpair first (pymobiledevice3 lockdown unpair) or reset trust as described above, then pair again.

docs.title: "Failed to start service" (InvalidServiceError)
docs.text:
The single most common error. A developer service was requested but the device can't provide it yet. In order:

  1. Enable Developer Mode (iOS 16+):

    pymobiledevice3 amfi enable-developer-mode

    This reboots the device. If it fails with "Cannot enable Developer Mode while the device has a passcode set" (DeviceHasPasscodeSetError), remove the device passcode temporarily — iOS refuses to enable Developer Mode automatically while one is set (you can instead enable it manually under Settings → Privacy & Security → Developer Mode).

  2. Mount the Developer Disk Image (DDI), the Apple-signed image that adds developer services to the device (once per boot). Every developer service needs it on iOS < 17; on iOS 17+, developer core-device needs it but developer dvt doesn't:

    pymobiledevice3 mounter auto-mount

    This downloads the correct image for your iOS version and caches it under ~/.pymobiledevice3 ($XDG_DATA_HOME/pymobiledevice3 on new Linux installs, %USERPROFILE%\.pymobiledevice3 on Windows) — no Xcode required. From iOS 27 the image is the Cryptex1 DDI, installed over cryptexd just like pymobiledevice3 cryptex auto-install; it also covers devices newer than the DDI itself. That needs an RSD (RemoteServiceDiscovery) tunnel, which auto-mount sets up by itself (see the CLI recipes).

  3. On iOS 17+, developer commands also need a tunnel — but you normally don't need to do anything: the CLI establishes a no-root userspace tunnel in-process automatically (you'll see a "Trying again over a no-root userspace tunnel" message, which is normal). The exception is iOS 17.0-17.3 on Linux/Windows, which needs a running tunneld (see below). See iOS 17+ tunnels for the full picture.

docs.title: "does not offer the ... service, which its DeveloperDiskImage provides" (DeveloperDiskImageServiceError)
docs.text:
The com.apple.coredevice.* services (developer core-device: screenshots, HID input, apps, files, ...) are not part of iOS: daemons inside the mounted DeveloperDiskImage provide them, so which ones the device offers depends on that image. The error says which case applies:

  • "none is mounted" — mount one with pymobiledevice3 mounter auto-mount. The image is unmounted by every reboot, including the one an iOS update ends with.

  • "the mounted one (...) does not include it" — an older image is mounted, for example by an older Xcode on the same host. The Xcode 26 images, for instance, lack com.apple.coredevice.screencaptureservice and com.apple.coredevice.hid.universalhidservice, which the Xcode 27 ones add. Replace it with the one this release expects; no Xcode is needed:

    pymobiledevice3 cryptex uninstall com.apple.MobileAsset.DDI   # if `cryptex list` shows it
pymobiledevice3 mounter umount-personalized                   # otherwise
pymobiledevice3 mounter auto-mount

    An older Xcode left running may mount its own image again when it sees the device.

docs.title: "DeveloperDiskImage already mounted" (AlreadyMountedError)
docs.text:
Nothing to fix: the image is already there and developer services can use it, so mounter auto-mount reports this at info level and exits 0, so scripts can run it unconditionally. It exits non-zero only when no image could be mounted. To replace it — for example with a newer DDI — remove it first. Which command applies depends on how it was mounted: cryptex list shows com.apple.MobileAsset.DDI only when it was installed as a cryptex (by auto-mount from iOS 27, cryptex auto-install, or Xcode):

pymobiledevice3 cryptex uninstall com.apple.MobileAsset.DDI   # installed as a cryptex
pymobiledevice3 mounter umount-personalized                   # mounted by the image mounter
pymobiledevice3 mounter umount-developer                      # iOS < 17

Older versions of cryptex auto-install did not notice an image mounted by the image mounter and failed late with "mkdir custom mount path: /System/Developer [17: File exists]". That is the same situation — remove the mounted image as above, or upgrade pymobiledevice3.

docs.title: "Trying again over ... since RSD is required for this command"
docs.text: A notice, not an error: the command needs an RSD tunnel, so the CLI retries over a no-root tunnel by itself. It appears for developer commands on iOS 17+ ("since it is a developer command on an iOS 17+ device"), and for mounter auto-mount from iOS 27, where the DeveloperDiskImage is installed as a cryptex over cryptexd, which is only reachable through an RSD tunnel. Pass --tunnel, --userspace or --native to pick the transport up front. If the retry itself fails, see iOS 17+ tunnels.

docs.title: "The image's build manifest has no entry for this device" (NoSuchBuildIdentityError)
docs.text: The device is newer than the DeveloperDiskImage — typically a newly released model such as the iPhone 18 series. The image mounter's PersonalizedDMG only lists the boards known when the DDI was built (Xcode 27.1's stops at iPhone18,5), so there is nothing to personalize for this one, and such devices can only use the Cryptex1 DDI, which has no such list. Upgrade pymobiledevice3: these devices run iOS 27 or later, where mounter auto-mount installs the cryptex.

docs.title: "does not install the DeveloperDiskImage as a cryptex" / "asset already present: Cryptex1,GenericVolume"
docs.text:
iOS installs the DeveloperDiskImage as a cryptex only from 26.4. Below it, cryptexd may import the image but the kernel does not let it mount one at /System/Developer, and its asset-type table is ordered differently, so the install fails: older pymobiledevice3 versions crashed cryptexd there ("asset already present: Cryptex1,GenericVolume", followed by a bare "Aborted.") (#1991). Below iOS 26.4 use pymobiledevice3 mounter auto-mount, which mounts the PersonalizedDMG, and upgrade if an older pymobiledevice3 (11.19.0 - 11.19.2) took the cryptex path there.

If cryptex auto-install fails on iOS 26.4 or later with "cryptexd closed the connection without replying", capture pymobiledevice3 syslog live -m cryptexd while running it and open an issue with both.

docs.title: "Unable to connect to tunneld" (TunneldConnectionError)
docs.text:
You passed --tunnel (or the automatic fallback chose tunneld — which happens on Linux/Windows with iOS 17.0–17.3, where the userspace tunnel has no reliable transport; macOS serves those devices no-root via the native tunnel), but no tunneld daemon is running. Start one with root privileges in a separate terminal and leave it running:

sudo "$(which pymobiledevice3)" remote tunneld

On Windows, run pymobiledevice3 remote tunneld from an Administrator terminal instead. See Running with sudo for why the full path is needed on Linux.

docs.title: "This command requires root privileges" / "admin privileges" (AccessDeniedError)
docs.text: The requested operation needs elevated privileges — typically creating a kernel tunnel (remote start-tunnel, remote tunneld). Re-run with sudo (macOS/Linux; see Running with sudo) or from an Administrator shell (Windows). For developer commands, prefer the default no-root userspace tunnel instead — it requires no privileges at all.

docs.title: PskCipherNotSupportedError
docs.text:
Your Python's SSL backend cannot negotiate the PSK ciphers the TCP tunnel requires — typical for interpreters linked against LibreSSL, such as Apple's /usr/bin/python3. Reinstall on a uv-managed Python, which is linked against OpenSSL:

uv tool install --reinstall --managed-python pymobiledevice3

Or use any other Python build linked against OpenSSL (e.g. the python.org installer, or brew install python).

docs.title: QuicProtocolNotSupportedError
docs.text: Apple removed QUIC tunnel support in iOS 18.2+. Drop the QUIC protocol selection (--protocol quic) and use a TCP tunnel (--protocol tcp).

docs.title: "Web Inspector is disabled" (WebInspectorNotEnabledError)
docs.text: Enable it on the device: Settings → Apps → Safari → Advanced → Web Inspector (on iOS 17 and earlier, Settings → Safari → Advanced).

docs.title: "Remote Automation is disabled" (RemoteAutomationNotEnabledError)
docs.text: Automation commands (webinspector launch, webinspector js-shell --automation, webinspector shell) additionally require Remote Automation in the same Advanced menu.

docs.title: Encrypted backups
docs.text: If the device has backup encryption enabled, commands that read backup contents need the password: pass --password (-p) to backup2 subcommands. A BackupFilterPasswordRequiredError means you combined a filtered backup with --patch-manifest on an encrypted backup — that also requires --password, so the manifest can be decrypted and re-encrypted.

docs.title: "device asked the host to free N bytes"
docs.text:
The device decided the backup destination is too small and asked the host to make room (DLMessagePurgeDiskSpace). pymobiledevice3 has no way to reclaim space on your behalf, so it answers "failed to purge" — exactly like Apple's own host does when its purge fails — and lets the device report what it wants to do next.

Free up at least the requested number of bytes and retry. Note that the first filtered backup still transfers all backup bytes from the device (filtering saves disk, not transfer) — budget space accordingly.

Run with -vv to also see the figure the host reported for DLMessageGetFreeDiskSpace; that is the number the device compared against, and it comes from statvfs on the backup directory (on macOS, raised to the purgeable-aware capacity Finder uses).

docs.title: "Manifest references files not in backup" (InvalidBackupError, MBErrorDomain/205)
docs.text:
When a backup finishes transferring, the device lists the backup directory on this computer and checks it against the new Manifest.db. If a file the manifest lists is not there, it fails the backup with MBErrorDomain/205 — after the progress bar reached 100%. The device uses the same code for other contradictions in the backup directory (an unknown SnapshotState in Status.plist, a missing file encryption key, a password that does not match the manifest), and the message carries its wording.

A backup directory that is already incomplete when the backup starts does not cause this: the device runs the same check before an incremental backup and, when it fails, quietly makes a full backup instead. The error means files went missing by the time the backup finished — something removed or changed them while it was running (a sync or cleanup tool, another backup into the same directory, a script that moves payload files away).

Run the backup again and leave the directory alone until it finishes: the device sends everything that is missing. If it keeps failing, pass --full or back up into an empty directory.

docs.title: Still stuck?
docs.text:
• Re-run with -vv and read the debug logs.
  • Search the GitHub issues.
